ae.title: Hold Off on Signing
ae.brief: The hot Americano launches next Monday. Manager Wu has already promised his boss a full wall at MRT City Hall Station. The vendor will only hold it until 9, and the contract only guarantees that the ad goes up.

lines.text: The contract came through just as I got to the gates. They'll only hold the wall until 9, and the deposit is due today.
I told my boss yesterday we'd have the whole wall by next Monday. Now he wants to know how many extra cups we'll sell.
Manager Wu, the contract only gives us a posting date. Can we check what number your boss will look at when he signs off?
Cups sold. Last time I showed him foot traffic and he asked if everyone coming out of the station had bought a coffee.
I just checked for you. The store can tally cups sold at the promo price, but the manager needs instructions by noon today.
Got it. I'll put the decisions we need by 9 in writing for you. I'll be on the call with you, too.

steps.prompt: Which plan do you ask Manager Wu to take to his boss before 9?

options.text: Hold the whole wall. Get the boss to sign off on buying launch visibility, then ask Creative to rush the print job.
options.feedback: On Monday, the boss snaps a photo of the whole wall along the bus terminal passage and posts it in the company chat. Creative was still making changes just before the print shop closed last night, and the weekly sales report shows only a slight bump in cups sold.
options.insight: Posterscope found that 83% of shoppers had seen an out-of-home ad in the 30 minutes before shopping.

options.text: Move the budget to morning digital slots. Run the Americano deal during the commute and ask the store to tally discounted cups separately.
options.feedback: On Monday morning the store manager reports that the Americano deal is beating expectations. The next day the screen shows the old price, so you're up early getting the vendor to swap the file and asking staff to honor the deal at the register.
options.insight: The 2018 yearbook identifies three keys to the evolution of out-of-home advertising in Taiwan: measurement, automated trading, and dynamic delivery.

options.text: Tell the boss up front that the full wall won't tell him how many extra cups he sold. Switch the contract to a small board by the exit and test the deal at the nearest store only.
options.feedback: The boss stares at the smaller placement mockup for a while, then agrees to start with one store. After launch, Manager Wu takes the store's discounted cup count into his meeting and texts to thank you for joining that call.
options.insight: The 2018 yearbook recommends starting with a small, workable version of an omnichannel experience and improving it over time.

ae.title: Call Back Before Noon
ae.brief: HQ at Itch Be Gone is taking a drop in searches as a drop in sales. Procurement is waiting on the change order, and Manager Chen needs a line he can take into his meeting.

lines.text: Chen meets with Finance at noon. He circled the numbers and asked if he should cut stock because searches are down.
The change order's next to your keyboard. The media team's holding tonight's slot until eleven thirty. Keeping it takes a signature.
He just told Finance last night they'd sell through the stock. I'll text him now and call by eleven thirty so he has time to fix his deck.
The contract only covers the original buy. Get his signature for any extra spend, and don't promise sales over the phone.
I'll stop by the convenience store on Songshou Road. Last time we met, he kept asking who actually buys this stuff in stores.

steps.hint: Songshou Rd. Corner Convenience Store: who's buying Itch Be Gone?

lines.text: Ning, got a sec? Who's been buying Itch Be Gone lately? What do they ask for when they walk in?
A delivery guy on the morning shift dropped his old box on the counter and asked if we had more. I grabbed one from under the register.
Why's it under the register? The spot on the shelf is empty.
We sold out last night. This box only came in this morning. If you're telling HQ, remember this is just one store.
Got it. I'll put that in my notes. Chen just messaged me on LINE asking if he can put 'demand is down' in his deck.

steps.prompt: It's eleven twenty, and you're under the awning outside the store. Chen picks up. What do you ask him to get approved at noon?

options.text: Get him to sign off on three days of extra search and social ads and send shoppers to the in-stock online store tonight.
options.feedback: You keep the evening slot, and the online store picks up orders over the next three days. When Finance asks why stores are still sitting on stock, Chen realizes the ads only send people online and asks you to spell that out in the change order.
options.insight: The yearbook calls this blind spot the caveman effect. If you only look at the data that survives, it's easy to mistake a piece of the picture for the whole thing.

options.text: Ask him to change 'demand is down' to 'searches are down,' hold the extra spend, and give you until tomorrow morning to bring in rainfall and store sales data.
options.feedback: Chen tells Finance what you actually know. They give you a day, and tonight's slot goes back on the market. You and Ah-Kai bring in the rainfall and store sales figures the next day, and Chen asks you to sit in on budget meetings from now on.
options.insight: In the yearbook's nail fungus treatment case, there were nearly 30% fewer rainy days than the year before. The consultant's report overlooked local conditions.

options.text: Ask him to approve a one-week store pilot. You'll get three stores to put up counter signs and log what customers ask for.
options.feedback: Three stores agree to put the Itch Be Gone name on the counter, and customers start pointing to the sign and asking about it the next day. You visit during the evening shift to collect notes and chase restocks, with customer feedback to share this week and sales figures still pending.
options.insight: The yearbook argues for pairing big data with sample surveys, retail interviews, and small data to see customers who leave no trace online.

ae.title: Rewrite the Contract Before Noon
ae.brief: With the pandemic, Chen’s boss wants the whole budget spent on driving traffic. The contract says ad performance includes both in-store and online orders. You have until noon to agree with Chen on how to rewrite that clause.

lines.text: Look at page seven. Yesterday I swore to my boss we could tell which in-store orders came from the ads.
Now he wants the whole budget on traffic. This morning he sent me an article about cookies going away and asked if I'd sign off on that number.
I can help you walk him through it this afternoon, Chen. Hold off on sending this for signature at noon. Let me find out which orders we can actually match.
My worry is that Finance sees a number and reads it as a guarantee. If we're one order short, they'll tell me to make up that order.
I'll spell out exactly what you can sign off on. You'll see the revised clause first.
Find Ah-Kai at Lanshan Plaza. He's got last year's order files. I'll send you a photo of page seven.

steps.hint: Go to Lanshan Plaza Data Lab and see if the client's data is usable

lines.text: Online orders have campaign codes. The store file only has receipt numbers. Right now there's no way to match those up with the ad report.
What if we try a dedicated coupon at one store? Could we give Chen redemption figures next Friday?
If the manager can put someone on cashier training today, we'll have the first week's numbers next Friday. I can't give you figures for every store.
The brand video is almost final, too. If we're keeping that budget, we need Chen to get someone to make the call in this meeting.
Okay, let's strike the line about counting every in-store order. I'll bring the original contract so Chen can compare the two versions.

steps.prompt: Chen puts page seven of the contract up on the meeting-room screen. Which version do you ask him to sign?

options.text: Put the whole budget into online promotions and use campaign orders for sign-off. Pause the brand video for this campaign.
options.feedback: The online sale goes live before month-end, and the orders close the gap. Chen uses the report to request payment. With the brand video pulled, the social page has only discount graphics to post for this campaign.
options.insight: In January 2020, Google announced that Chrome would phase out third-party cookies within two years. At the time, Chrome held nearly 70% of Taiwan's browser market.

options.text: Explain face-to-face why the store orders can't be matched. Keep the online promotion and one short brand video, then arrange a dedicated coupon pilot with one store manager.
options.feedback: Chen rewrites the acceptance clause on the spot, and Finance agrees to start with online orders and coupon redemptions at the pilot store. Next Friday, you bring Chen the first redemption breakdown, and the smaller promotion budget means online orders are growing a little more slowly.
options.insight: In a Salesforce survey, 84% of customers said the content, interactions, and service a brand provides at each touchpoint are as important as the product itself.

options.text: Protect the brand video and reach budget, and push the sales target back. Ask Chen to name one point of contact for video approval today, with reach and orders signed off separately.
options.feedback: The video goes live on schedule and brand reach rises, but orders still come up short at month-end. Finance asks you to explain the gap next week, and you're chasing sign-offs from Legal and Retail every evening.
options.insight: Third-party research found that 65% of Adidas sales came from brand activity. Adidas shifted its brand-to-performance budget split from 23:77 to 60:40.

ae.title: Please Confirm by Four
ae.brief: The real estate client wants to add a booking number to the brand film at the last minute, but the contract covers one 30-second spot. The Chillshan Creative Park studio has to be handed back at four. You need written approval before the crew can roll.

lines.text: Elephant Mountain View Realty just sent a screenshot. Their boss asked in the group chat who viewers should call to book a viewing after the ad.
Our marketing contact told me the brand film was approved this morning. Now she's worried her boss will put her on the spot at tonight's meeting.
We hand the studio back at four. Find out what we're actually shooting today so I know which shot to start with.
I found the contract attachment. It covers one 30-second spot. If we're delivering a second cut, someone needs to sign a change order today.
I'll call her first. If she's worried about getting cornered tonight, I'll join the meeting and spell out what we can deliver and what costs extra.
Okay. Customer service and the cast are still online. Get me that email and I'll roll.

steps.prompt: The client picks up. They need a commitment they can take into tonight's meeting. What do you offer?

options.text: Keep the price and deadline. Turn the 30 seconds into a virtual viewing demo and get written approval for the phone number on the end card.
options.feedback: Your contact signs off by email, the branches staff the phone, and a few viewings get booked on launch day. The original story scenes are cut, and hardly anyone shares the spot from the brand's social accounts.
options.insight: The yearbook says consumers can complete the whole shopping journey from home, so brands need fully digital operations and the ability to deliver to people's doors.

options.text: Keep the brand film. Flag that there's no booking number on the end card, and help your contact pitch brand favorability to the boss as the success metric.
options.feedback: The boss agrees to change the success metric and puts the film on the brand's homepage, where it gets more shares than expected. The branches report no bump in bookings, and you get another call about it the next day.
options.insight: In post-testing, 70% of viewers responded more positively after seeing Sinyi Realty's “Trust and Happiness,” compared with a past KPI of 20–30%.

options.text: Get a signed change order. Shoot a booking end card in the same studio session, then set separate deadlines and success metrics for the brand film and the short cut that drives bookings.
options.feedback: The client signs the change order, the brand film gets shared, and the short cut brings in bookings. The two department heads review their cuts separately, and you're up with production reconciling versions until the early hours.
options.insight: The yearbook says dentsu advocated breaking down service silos so creative, media, data, and consulting teams could work together.

ae.title: What Goes to Print at Four?
ae.brief: The Shin Kong Mitsukoshi sign is due at four, and Manager Hsu has just learned that the plastic reduction figure hasn't been cleared. As his AE, you need to agree on what you can deliver for the anniversary sale before the printer closes the job.

lines.text: Here's the proof for the anniversary sale. HQ just emailed. We can't use the plastic reduction figure yet.
I told my boss the refills would sell this week. If we pull the sign, he'll ask where the money went.
We can keep the counter spot, Manager Hsu. I'll hold the proof, but we need something printable by four.
I checked the contract. It covers one sign. Extra staff or a new spot needs a signed addendum today.
My meeting's at five. Give me one sentence I can take in there and say to my boss.
Okay. I'll tell you what we can deliver for the sale and send the meeting notes with it.

steps.prompt: The printer is waiting for the file. What do you ask Manager Hsu to sign off on today?

options.text: Put the weekend add-on price on the sign and get retail to approve a checkout discount on refills.
options.feedback: Retail clears the discount and more refills ring up over the weekend. The counter flips the sign back to full price the following week, and returning shoppers still ask for the deal.
options.insight: Kantar surveyed 500 people in Taiwan. Of those, 85% thought eco-friendly products were more expensive.

options.text: Say the figure hasn't cleared and get Hsu to sign off on two stages: print the instructions now, add the figure once it's verified.
options.feedback: Purchasing and QA spend two days checking the records, and you put the basis for the comparison and the revision date in the addendum. Hsu uses it to get through his meeting and copies you on the next round of approvals.
options.insight: In the same Kantar survey, 71% of respondents felt there wasn't enough information about eco-friendly products.

options.text: Get an addendum for a spot by the entrance, display the actual packaging, invite the press and have the brand send someone to answer questions.
options.feedback: A local news crew films the cutaway bottle and the refill pouch laid flat, and Hsu shares the clip in his managers' group chat. For two days straight you're there before opening and still on site after closing to oversee teardown.
options.insight: The report describes three stages of sustainability transformation: Compliance, Competency, and Competitiveness.

ae.title: Call Back Before Five
ae.brief: No-Overtime Milk Tea launches at 8 tomorrow morning. Franchisees are chasing the posters, but Ah-Kai has put the print files on hold at Lanshan Plaza.

lines.text: Hold off on sending the print files. I got to the last page and couldn't trace the pattern on the cup sleeve in the AI image.
The franchise group chat's already announced an 8 AM launch. The client even asked if they could reuse the image for next month's store opening.
The quote just says 'new product promotion.' It doesn't say where we can use AI or whether franchisees can print the artwork.
The client just messaged me. She's worried her boss will think she's holding things up. The printer needs files by five. Give her something she can take back to him.
I'll call. Can you ask Wei how many placements he can cover tonight with the photos we shot?
On it. Ask the client this, too. If she can only have one thing by morning, does she want the in-store poster or the order page?

steps.prompt: You owe the client a call before five. What can you agree to deliver?

options.text: Pull the AI image and rebuild the whole set tonight with product photos. Keep the launch on schedule and send the coupons a day later.
options.feedback: You're up with the designers past midnight. The opening crews get matching photo posters, and the brand's website gets the new look too. The coupons go out a day later, so the launch misses its planned push to drive orders.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that Coca-Cola's Masterpiece animation took eight weeks to make. Without AI, it could have taken five times as long.

options.text: Tell the client you can't trace the image, get written approval to use only product photos, and deliver the order page first thing tomorrow.
options.feedback: The client uses your confirmation email to brief her boss. She agrees to open orders on time and wait two days for the franchise posters. You and Ah-Kai spell out where AI is allowed and what franchisees can use, then send the contract addendum for sign-off.
options.insight: The yearbook flags three things for account executives to discuss with clients: where AI can be used, what the contract requires them to disclose, and who owns the rights.

options.text: Agree by phone to use the AI image on the order page to start taking orders. Hold the franchise print files until you've checked the source.
options.feedback: Orders start coming in at eight. Before noon, a franchisee has printed a screenshot as a table sign, and a customer posts asking whether it's a collaboration with another brand. The client calls to ask how it ended up in print, and you have to ring each store to get it taken down.
options.insight: The yearbook points out that AI makes content cheaper to produce and slower to verify. A check that once took a second might now take a minute, ten minutes, or even an hour.

ae.title: The Launch Is On. What Do We Tell HQ?
ae.brief: One Less Piece opens its Linginger Street flagship next week, with enough budget for one launch. The client told headquarters the neighborhood shops were on board, but nobody's signed.

lines.text: You're the AE on this. Look at the deck the client just sent HQ. It says the neighborhood shops are joining next week.
The contract only budgets for one launch. The client's worried HQ might pull the money and wants a confirmed list tonight.
I'll pull the shop names from the deck for now. I'll snap their storefronts on the way to the Fude Street shrine and check with Ah-Cheng.
Good. Call the client before the nine o'clock pitch so they know what's still up in the air before they present.

steps.hint: Walk the alleys to Fude St. Earth God Shrine. Note the old shops

lines.text: Ah-Cheng's by the red chairs with the shopkeepers' reply slips. You saw how narrow it is in front of the ice shop on your way here, right?

The ice shop owner saw the photos from the last opening. He doesn't want another line blocking his door. The fabric shop will lend us its window if the owner can approve the shop name and photos first.
I'll take the ice shop out. If the fabric shop only has to lend us the window and won't have to handle a line, how soon can we get their approval?
The fabric shop owner's in tonight. The tofu pudding stall won't get back to us till morning. They can't take vouchers when it's too busy, so agree on a daily cap up front.
Got it. I'll write down who can sign and when they can get back to us, so I have something concrete for the call.

steps.prompt: The client calls. "What can I actually leave on that slide for nine?" What do you tell them?

options.text: Ask the client to put the launch budget into the flagship. Offer an instant discount to drive week-one sales and take the neighborhood partnership off the slide.
options.feedback: The discount drives checkouts at the flagship, and the store manager reorders early. The client still has to walk back the promise to HQ and asks you to confirm every revision in writing from then on.
options.insight: The yearbook says the brand is where all marketing investment builds over time. It warns against chasing short-term traffic and results alone.

options.text: Renegotiate the deliverables. Scale down the opening promo, arrange a month-long co-branded window display with the fabric shop, and put the approval deadline in the contract addendum tonight.
options.feedback: The window goes up with the brand's fabric swatches and old photos of the shop, and local media come by twice to cover it. Without the big discount, week-one sales tick up only slightly. You spend two nights waiting until closing to get both sides to sign off on how they're credited.
options.insight: In the yearbook's UNIQLO East District case, the neighborhood partnership hit 105% of its sales target and drew 2.2 times as many visitors as the year before.

options.text: Tell the client the shops haven't signed. Ask them to approve a paper tofu pudding voucher with a minimum purchase, and hold printing until the stall owner signs off on the redemption cap.
options.feedback: The client uses your approval timetable to brief HQ and keeps the launch budget. The stall owner signs off on the cap the next day, and shoppers add items to qualify for the voucher. You tally the stubs daily and tell the cashiers to take down the sign when the vouchers run out.
options.insight: The yearbook calls for inclusive customer experiences and says an omnichannel approach should account for older shoppers and customers with established shopping habits.

ae.title: Sign Off by Eight
ae.brief: The soy sauce client thinks TV costs too much and wants next year's budget moved online. Ms. Su needs an answer on the premiere slot by eight.

lines.text: The boss upstairs says zero TV next year. But we need a signature by eight to keep this slot.
The brand manager asked me privately to hang on to it. He promised the retailer a TV spot the week the new bottle hits shelves.
He's worried they'll pull the display. His boss is worried he'll spend the money and have no order numbers to show for it. No wonder all I got back was a sticker.
I checked with creative. The old spot shows the old bottle. A last-minute change to the end card costs extra.
I'll bring that up first. Ms. Su, how firm was the promise he made to the retailer?
I'll forward the message. You've got time to stop by the breakfast shop on the corner and see how different the bottles look side by side.

steps.hint: Wuxing St. Corner Breakfast Shop: what's everyone watching on TV?

lines.text: Perfect timing. A customer pointed at that soy sauce ad on TV and asked about it, so I got this bottle out to show them.
Auntie, there are two kinds on the shelf. Which one did you grab?
The red cap's the old one. Yesterday someone came looking for the bottle from TV. The new one was right there and they walked straight past it.
I'll get a picture of the bottles. I need to tell the client people might still look for the wrong one if we run the old spot.
Get the one on the right. I used the one on the left to prop up the remote, and the cap's all sticky.

steps.prompt: The hold is about to expire. What can you take upstairs that the brand manager can get signed?

options.text: Drop the premiere slot and fund launch coupons. Call the retailer with the brand manager tonight to revise the deal.
options.feedback: The retailer takes the coupon promo in place of the premiere and keeps the display. Coupon orders come in fast the first week, but by month's end the retailer says plenty of shoppers still don't recognize the new bottle.
options.insight: The yearbook warns that narrowly targeted digital ads can miss older shoppers who do the family's grocery shopping.

options.text: Ask Ms. Su to keep the premiere slot, agree on the end-card fee with the client, and run the digital coupons as scheduled.
options.feedback: The brand manager gets approval, and the retailer gets the ad with the new bottle. Shoppers start asking for the new bottle specifically, and people still redeem the coupons. You stay with the creative team until the client approves the end card, just in time for the station's delivery deadline.
options.insight: The yearbook cites a Dentsu Group estimate for audiences aged 30 and up: TV CPM is about 48, while YouTube ads typically range from 80 to 250.

options.text: Show the hold and the recut fee, pitch a single test slot, and agree to wait for new-customer counts before booking the rest.
options.feedback: Once the boss hears the production costs and measurement limits, he signs off on the test and holds the rest of the budget for review. The retailer delays the extra coupons, so early orders take a hit. You're on calls with the retailer and the data team every week to reconcile the new-customer counts.
options.insight: The yearbook warns that a strong brand lift result may just reflect people who already support the brand.

ae.title: Hold That Email
ae.brief: The client plans to announce a pilot for its AI shopping agent tomorrow morning. A test order just showed that the agent can swap out an out-of-stock item and check out on its own. Lin wants you to reply before the pitch.

lines.text: You’re the AE on this. The client scheduled the launch email for nine tomorrow and wants a yes or no from me.
I printed the contract. They signed off on recommendations for this phase, but the announcement says it can buy a replacement if something’s out of stock.
I just ran a test order. Oat milk was out, so it swapped in regular milk and placed the order without asking.
Their e-commerce lead is worried sales will fall flat tomorrow. PR’s already sent the release to the press, so someone will have to call around if it changes.
They’re asking for slide nine in the conference room. Get back to the client first. Who signs off tonight, and what goes live in the morning?
Mei, can you see who’s still online in e-commerce and support? I’ll spell out which line in the announcement needs changing.

steps.prompt: Lin leaves the cursor on “Please confirm we’re good to launch.” What do you send back?

options.text: Keep checkout on for nine, limit it to in-stock items, and get the client to sign off on the revised pilot scope tonight.
options.feedback: Orders come in on schedule, bringing in more sales than recommendations alone. The client only realizes after signing that the promised out-of-stock substitutions are gone and asks you to review each item with them before future launches.
options.insight: The yearbook describes four levels of agent authority: observe and understand, recommend, decide, and act. Walmart’s Sparky can handle shopping tasks across categories.

options.text: Call the client about the failed test, get their approval to launch recommendations only, and book a separate sign-off for checkout.
options.feedback: You go through the announcement line by line with e-commerce and support, and your client contact takes the revised copy to their boss. Recommendations still send shoppers to product pages, but after the pitch you’re back at your desk filling out the sign-off checklist.
options.insight: The yearbook describes three ways to build trust into the agent experience: previewing what the agent intends to do, auditing its actions, and providing a way to escalate.

options.text: Ask PR to turn tomorrow’s launch announcement into an invitation for a limited preview, with purchases disabled on the trial page.
options.feedback: You help PR call each outlet with the revised copy, and the coverage brings in another batch of sign-ups. E-commerce loses the first day of orders, and the client calls you back to renegotiate the launch date.
options.insight: In the 2025 CMO Report, which surveyed more than 1,950 CMOs, 90% said strong brand preference was key to winning.

planner.title: Coffee Before the Bus
planner.brief: The hot Americano launches next week. The boss wants to run “Strong enough to wake you up” at City Hall Station. Manager Wu sends you to ask commuters how they really pick their morning coffee.

lines.text: “Strong enough to wake you up” topped the tasting survey. My boss wants it sent to the billboard printer by noon.
I asked three people at Exit 2. All three said they liked strong coffee. Two took one look at the line and walked off.
I asked those two where they were headed. Their bus was due, and they weren't about to gamble on what everyone ahead of them might order.
My sticky note said “not strong enough.” Now I want to know how many minutes they'd spare for coffee.
I can take that back to the office. But when my boss asks, what have I got to show him?
I'll put the tasting survey next to our notes from the exit. First we need to pick what we want this Americano launch to prove.

steps.prompt: There's time to send one proposal before noon. What will you take to Manager Wu?

options.text: Interview regulars waiting by the exit and turn the little breaks they squeeze in into a line: “Take a seat before work.”
options.feedback: It takes three mornings of follow-up interviews to pull together enough commuter quotes for the station posters. Nearby office workers share photos in their work chats, and some even use the line to invite coworkers on a break. The store sells only a few more hot Americanos in week one.
options.insight: Intelligent Decision suggests looking past the initial brief. Start with the experience you want people to have, then find the medium that can deliver it.

options.text: Test “Order your hot Americano ahead and grab it as you leave the station.” Give advance orders their own line during the rush.
options.feedback: The store sells more hot Americanos during the morning rush in week one, and the manager moves the pickup table closer to the door. You spend the next few mornings at the store sorting out the pickup order so the two lines stop getting in each other's way.
options.insight: In its discussion of omnichannel retail, Intelligent Decision recommends mapping the customer journey to find where it breaks down, then starting with a small test you can actually run.

options.text: Take Manager Wu to interview commuters at the exit, then test “Just around the corner from the station” at one store to see who makes the detour.
options.feedback: Manager Wu hears someone say they like strong coffee, then immediately ask how close the store is. Morning sales edge up at the test store, and the other stores miss the first wave. She takes your interview notes into the meeting and gets the original tagline put on hold.
options.insight: The 2018 edition points out that what people say can differ from what they do. Neuromarketing can fill gaps in surveys, but an artificial test setting can still skew results.

planner.title: The Blue Tube
planner.brief: HQ thinks customers have forgotten the brand because searches are down. They want new packaging and more ads, and Chief Lin wants you to find out how shoppers recognize the ointment before noon.

lines.text: HQ at Itch Be Gone says searches are down so far that people must have forgotten the brand.
The new box just came in. They took out the blue and put the brand name in huge letters on the front.
It goes to print at noon. You're the strategist. Who needs to see the name that big?
I want to hear what customers actually say when they get to the counter.
Try the convenience store on Songshou Road. Take the sample, but let the clerk talk before you show it.

steps.hint: Songshou Rd. Corner Convenience Store: who's buying Itch Be Gone?

lines.text: Do you remember what the last person who bought Itch Be Gone said when he came in?
The guy in rain boots this morning? He put his empty tube on the counter and asked for another blue one before he got off work.
What about first-time buyers? Do they ask for the blue one too?
Yesterday someone typed 'feet itch in my shoes' on his phone and showed me. He kept the screen dim. He didn't want the people in line hearing him ask out loud.
I've got both phrases on the back of the box now. Bet the first thing HQ asks in the meeting is how big the brand name should be.

steps.prompt: Chief Lin texts, 'Can the box go to print?' Which proposal do you send back first?

options.text: Print the old box for now. Use 'feet itch in your shoes?' in search ads to reach people already looking for ointment.
options.feedback: More people buy the ointment online that week. When HQ asks at month-end how many shoppers still recognize the old box in stores, all you have is Ning's one example.
options.insight: The yearbook uses the caveman effect to show how relying on records that survive can leave out people who never made it into those records.

options.text: Ask HQ to hold printing for a week. Have regulars find the product with both boxes, and ask when they last bought it.
options.feedback: Regulars grab the old box and head for the register. When they see the sample, they ask Ning if the medicine has changed. HQ reviews the notes, keeps the blue, and lets stores keep selling as usual.
options.insight: In the yearbook's nail fungus treatment case, there were nearly 30% fewer rainy days than the year before. Local conditions matter when you're trying to explain shifts in demand.

options.text: Cover the morning and evening shifts, interview new and repeat buyers, and draft a shelf card shoppers can point to.
options.feedback: The morning crowd talks about sweaty rain boots. Several evening shoppers are buying for family and bring the empty tubes. You finish the card after closing, and the retailer agrees to try it for a week, pushing back the first print run.
options.insight: The yearbook recommends filling gaps in big data with sample surveys, retail interviews, and small data. The records you can get only cover part of the picture.

planner.title: Two Bottles in the Cart
planner.brief: Chen wants a promotion to revive sales during the pandemic. Before the noon meeting, find out why shoppers keep leaving two bottles of supplements in their carts.

lines.text: My boss wants a proposal at noon. Think we can run that “pandemic special: buy two, get one free” ad?
Lately people keep putting two bottles in their carts and leaving. Sales thinks the price has them walking away.
Hold off on changing the price. One shopper took a picture of the bottom of a bottle before checkout. I want to know what he was checking.
Go see Kai at Lanshan Plaza. He has last year’s orders, and I asked customer service to forward their follow-up notes.

steps.hint: Go to Lanshan Plaza Data Lab and see if the client's data is usable

lines.text: I found the follow-up for that shopper. Two bottles in the cart, only one on the receipt.
Did he say why he dropped the other one?
He said, “I was comparing the two. My mom still has some left, and I didn’t want to get her more of the same thing.”
So he needed someone to help him read the label. Chen asked me for a promotion, but he needs to hear this first.

steps.prompt: There’s room for one proposal in the noon deck. What do you pitch?

options.text: Offer a one-bottle trial with an instant credit at checkout, and spend the budget on shoppers close to buying.
options.feedback: Orders pick up this quarter, and Chen takes the sales report to his boss. As soon as the credit ends, support starts hearing, “How are you different from the brand next to you?” again.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that younger consumers like comparing prices and find direct cash credits more appealing than prize draws or discounts.

options.text: Take Chen to watch people shop at two pharmacies and pilot a card that helps them compare labels.
options.feedback: At the counter, Chen hears a shopper ask about a bottle they brought from home and agrees to a pilot on the spot. A few shoppers buy a bottle after the pharmacists use the card to walk them through the ingredients. For two weeks, you revise the card daily using feedback from both stores.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that shoppers for supplements and related health products prefer having someone explain them. At pharmacies, they look to the pharmacist for a recommendation.

options.text: Reposition the brand around “Know what’s in the bottle before you buy for family,” test it with caregivers, then launch the new packaging.
options.feedback: After the new packaging launches, a few caregiver groups start sharing the brand’s illustrated guide to reading labels. The redesign displaces a promotion, leaving a dent in this quarter’s sales. You spend six weeks with creative and retail teams getting the packaging and the in-store message to match.
options.insight: Adidas found that 65% of sales came from brand campaigns and shifted its brand-to-performance budget ratio from 23:77 to 60:40.

planner.title: Not Ready for a Viewing
planner.brief: Real estate bookings are down during the Level 3 COVID alert. Wei needs you to figure out who the brand film is for and what to tell them before the Chillshan Creative Park studio rental ends.

lines.text: Come here a sec. Sales says bookings are down because nobody knows we do virtual viewings.
They already printed the booking card. It’s right next to your coffee.
I talked to three first-time buyers on LINE this morning. They know about virtual viewings. They’re worried one question will get an agent chasing them to book.
And that card says “Book Now.” No wonder you’ve left it face down.
One guy just wanted to see out the window. He wanted to check the traffic downstairs before talking to an agent.
We lose the studio at four. Give me a line we can shoot, and something I can take back to Sales.

steps.prompt: How will you use page four of tonight’s pitch to get the client to drop “Book Now”?

options.text: Speak to people already house hunting. Offer virtual viewings at a time they can pick.
options.feedback: Sales checks the roster and signs off. The film brings in a few more bookings, but hardly anyone shares it, and most comments just ask what slots are left.
options.insight: The yearbook says home commerce can bring the entire customer journey into the home. The details of the service shape how people feel about it.

options.text: Position the brand around “Take your time. Ask when you’re ready,” starting with a buyer who just wants to see out the window.
options.feedback: You and Wei tweak the voice-over right up to the deadline. Once it’s live, people send the “ask when you’re ready” line to friends who are house hunting. Sales checks the next day and finds fewer bookings than the previous cut.
options.insight: The yearbook uses Sinyi Realty’s “Trust and Happiness” to show what a real story can do. The film deliberately left out the sales pitch, and seven in ten viewers showed a positive shift in the post-test.

options.text: Test the messages separately with people just starting their search and people already booking viewings.
options.feedback: You and Kai compare interview transcripts until midnight and find two different worries: people just starting out dread the follow-ups, and people ready to book can’t find a slot after work. The client agrees to lead with “ask when you’re ready” in the brand film and show open slots on the booking page.
options.insight: The yearbook warns analysts to distinguish what they observe from what’s really driving it.

planner.title: The Pump She Kept
planner.brief: Refills are gathering dust at Shin Kong Mitsukoshi. Manager Hsu wants you, the strategy planner, to find a message shoppers will actually listen to.

lines.text: My boss wants "Better for the planet" in bigger print. You handle strategy. Do you think that line can turn sales around?
I spoke with three people at the counter who bought a full bottle. One of them pulled a clean old pump out of her bag.
I saw that. She asked if she could still use it. The clerk wasn’t sure, so she took a full bottle to the register.
She went to the trouble of bringing it. I want to know if she was worried it wouldn’t fit or that it might leak.
My boss already put that planet line on slide one. What are you bringing him tomorrow morning?
I’ll bring the pump. First, let’s decide what we can actually promise shoppers.

steps.prompt: You can pitch one direction tomorrow morning. How do you give shoppers the confidence to switch to refills?

options.text: Lead with "Bring in your old pump. If it fits, grab a refill." Have the clerk check the fit at the counter.
options.feedback: Over the weekend, shoppers who’d picked up a full bottle switched to a refill on the spot after the fit check. Manager Hsu saw more refill sales, but all shoppers remembered afterward was that the clerk would check for them.
options.insight: The yearbook cites a Kantar survey in which 76% of Taiwanese respondents said convenience and cost kept them from taking environmental action.

options.text: Borrow older bottles to check fit and leakage, then make a card listing which pump models can be reused.
options.feedback: You and Kai borrowed old bottles from every counter and finished testing at closing time. Manager Hsu took the results into the meeting, and his boss agreed to lead with "You can keep using these pumps." Some shoppers took a photo of the card to check at home, and only a few extra refills sold that day.
options.insight: The yearbook cites a Kantar survey in which 71% of Taiwanese respondents felt companies gave them too little information about eco-friendly products.

options.text: Ask longtime customers to bring their old bottles to the counter for a short video about how long they’ve kept their pumps.
options.feedback: One customer brought a bottle covered in her daughter’s stickers, and the department store shared her interview on Facebook. People started posting pictures of their own bottles, but few of the people who came to watch bought anything. You spent two weekends interviewing shoppers and your evenings checking every pump model shown on camera.
options.insight: The yearbook says content is more likely to get noticed on social media when it feels relevant, gives people something of value, and makes them feel something.

planner.title: Who Is the Second Cup For?
planner.brief: The new drink goes on sale at 8 tomorrow morning. Kai brings you an AI interview summary and asks what No-Overtime Milk Tea should lead with.

lines.text: The AI put “worried it’ll be too sweet” at the top of its summary of the walk-up interviews at Lanshan Plaza. You’re the planner. Would you lead with that?
The client’s already stuck “Less Sugar” on the menu board. He wants an answer by five.
I spent half an hour at the Songgao Road shop. This woman ordered half sugar, so why did she add another cup just before paying?
Hang on, I’ll pull up the transcript. She said, “I was worried my coworker would find it too sweet.” Yep, two different sugar levels.
I asked her about it. Her coworker was still wrapping up a project, so she was taking a cup back to give them a break.
Okay, I’ll get them to hold the menu board. We owe the client a line he can put on it by five.

steps.prompt: The client needs the wording locked by five. What do you do with the receipt and interview?

options.text: Lead with “Bring a cup to someone still working.” Interview the evening crowd, then give that line the space reserved for the discount.
options.feedback: You finish typing up the extra interviews after closing, and Wei stays with you until almost dawn to get the wording right. The next day, someone snaps a photo of the line and sends it to a coworker, but you lose the orders a launch discount would have brought in.
options.insight: The yearbook warns that when everyone uses the same AI, the work tends toward the average. A team with varied talent is what gives a business a lasting edge.

options.text: Play the recording for the client and compare the two sugar levels. Test “Choose the sweetness for each cup” at one shop first.
options.feedback: You and Kai cross-check receipts half the evening, and the client crosses out “Less Sugar” himself after hearing the recording. The test shop gets a few extra two-cup orders, and the client asks you to run the next round of interviews.
options.insight: The yearbook calls first-party data the foundation for making money with AI. Poor-quality input leads to poor-quality output.

options.text: Launch tomorrow morning with NT$10 off the second cup. Save the coworker message for the next campaign.
options.feedback: Two-cup orders take off in the morning, but by lunch all anyone is sharing in group chats is a screenshot of the discount. The client asks what you’ll say next time without a deal, and you’re still sorting through comments after closing.
options.insight: The yearbook identifies four kinds of friction for shoppers: money, time, physical effort, and mental effort. Generative AI is especially good at saving mental effort.

planner.title: A Change Before Dinner
planner.brief: One Less Piece opens its flagship on Linginger Street next week. The client wants to spend the entire launch budget on a photo spot. Mei-ling asks you to find out what would actually get night market customers into a clothing store.

lines.text: You're our strategist. Take a look at this. The client sent three photos of neon walls. They figure if young people line up here, they'll line up for a photo too.
Those two in uniform took their chicken and left. Ah-Cheng, are they always in that much of a hurry?
They meet friends over by the Earth God shrine after work. Go ask them yourself. I've got a batch to pull out.
Go on. Before the nine o'clock pitch, I need to know where we're putting that launch money.

steps.hint: Walk the alleys to Fude St. Earth God Shrine. Note the old shops

lines.text: I asked two people outside the shrine who'd just clocked out. They were headed to dinner, and one was looking up where he could change nearby.
The guy holding his uniform? Last time he rode home, changed his shirt, then came back to meet his friends.
He said his uniform smelled like fryer oil, and he felt awkward showing up like that. I was all set to ask him where he takes photos.
Did you ask how far home is? By the time he's back, his fried chicken's gone soggy.
I'm pulling the photo-wall sticky note. These two want to go straight from work to dinner. That's the thought I'd build on.
Two people is enough for a hunch. The client has to settle on a launch tonight. Which idea are you asking them to back?

steps.prompt: You can pitch one plan tonight. What do you do with what you heard at the shrine?

options.text: Lead with ‘Change before dinner.’ Push tops that are in stock and run an after-work bundle deal in week one.
options.feedback: The pre-dinner bundles sell fastest, and the staff restock the popular sizes twice. As soon as the deal ends, hardly anyone asks about it, and the client pulls out the wrap report and asks what sets the line apart from anyone else's sale.
options.insight: The yearbook says marketing investment builds up in the brand, and long-term brand strength helps sustain short-term performance.

options.text: Make the store the stop between work and dinner. Ask night market staff to try on clothes and photograph what they'd actually wear out after closing.
options.feedback: You wait for the stalls to close to finish the shoot, then spend the night checking permission for each photo. During opening week, someone walks in with a photo a friend sent and asks, ‘Is this the place I can come change after work?’ Only a few of the pieces in the photos sell that week.
options.insight: UNIQLO's East District partnership in the yearbook drew 2.2 times the previous year's visitors, and 91% of people said the store would bring them to the area more often.

options.text: Get the client to approve a two-night sales trial. Compare ‘Night market looks’ with ‘Change before dinner’ and use try-ons and purchases to pick the launch message.
options.feedback: You and the staff rotate both signs each night, then stay after closing to check the fitting notes against the receipts. More people buy after trying things on when ‘Change before dinner’ is up. The client reads the notes, signs off on the message, and saves the rest of the budget for the launch.
options.insight: The yearbook describes using A/B testing alongside digital twins as an application of first-party data.

planner.title: Soy Sauce on the Shopping List
planner.brief: The soy sauce client wants “Order in One Tap” to lead the launch. Su needs you upstairs at Big Dawn Dome Broadcast Center in twenty minutes with a line that captures what the brand should stand for.

lines.text: The boss printed out the checkout screenshot and circled “Order in One Tap.” You’re the strategist. Should we keep that line?
What he’s got there is an order. If you want him to change the line, bring him a reason.
Mei, let me ask around first. Who picked the last bottle, and why that one?
Try Auntie at the corner of Wuxing Street. She’s still making egg pancakes, and the TV’s on.

steps.hint: Wuxing St. Corner Breakfast Shop: what's everyone watching on TV?

lines.text: Auntie, you added something to your list as soon as that soy sauce ad came on. What did you write?
“Yellow cap.” Last time my son ordered on his phone, he got the red cap. One bite of the braised tofu and I could tell he’d switched it.
So now you write down what you want and have him order it?
Yep. When they poured it on TV just now, the tofu turned the same color mine does. So I wrote down the brand, too.
He places the order, but you pick the brand. Before you try a new bottle, you want to see how the food will turn out.
Go ahead and take a picture. Give it back after, though. I still have to send it to him.

steps.prompt: Su texts you to come upstairs. What goes on slide one?

options.text: “Running low on soy sauce?” Give repeat buyers a restock coupon and drive orders this week.
options.feedback: The boss signs off on the coupon that night, and repeat orders pick up the next day. At the end of the month, shoppers who haven’t bought it still can’t name the new product.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that algorithms tend to serve ads to the people most likely to convert.

options.text: “That familiar taste of home.” Show the tofu taking on color and the bottle on TV, then feature that same bottle on the mobile page.
options.feedback: The boss keeps the TV slot and asks for a test shoot this week. When a parent in the screening points at the yellow cap and asks where to buy it, you add the purchase link just before launch.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that digital ads aimed only at the target audience can miss older family members who do the household shopping.

options.text: Interview the cooks and the people who place orders separately, then test two rough cuts: one about easy ordering, one about the familiar taste of home.
options.feedback: The boss agrees to hold off on the final wording, so the first promotion slips, too. You and Su spend three evenings interviewing people, and on Friday the boss signs off on more testing after seeing who you recruited and what they actually said.
options.insight: The yearbook warns that Brand Lift may simply reflect people who already support the brand.

planner.title: Where She Wants to Go
planner.brief: A joint supplement brand wants to lead with “Buy it for your parents.” In an interview, a mom deletes the bottle her daughter put in the cart. Director Lin wants the planner to settle on a message before the pitch.

lines.text: The client's already put “Buy it for your parents” on the cover. Anything you'd change after watching the interview?
They're pointing to the AI simulation. They've even booked a Friday promo for the gift bundle.
I paused the interview right here. The daughter adds the bottle to the cart and her mom reaches over and deletes it.
I asked what she was doing this weekend. She wants to take the bus to Yongkang Street herself so her daughter won't have to take time off to drive her again.
So should I shelve that photo of the mom and daughter holding hands? The client called it moving just this afternoon.
Give me one line. The pitch client is already seated next door and slide nine is still blank.

steps.prompt: Director Lin slides the cover page over to you. Which direction do you ask the client to back first?

options.text: Keep the gift promo and lead with a trial pack. Put the ingredients and price per serving at the top of the product page.
options.feedback: The trial packs sell faster than expected on Friday, so the e-commerce lead orders another batch. Returns start coming in marked “My mom didn't ask for this,” and the marketing lead wants to know why you only tested with the people paying.
options.insight: In the yearbook's supplement ad simulation, people aged 45 and over preferred fact-based ads featuring a professional.

options.text: Interview a few moms and daughters separately, then watch how they shop at a pharmacy. Bring the footage to the client and revise the message together.
options.feedback: After two nights at pharmacies, you find that some moms want to choose for themselves and others do ask their daughters to shop for them. The marketing lead watches two clips and agrees to use half the ad space to test a version aimed at the people who take the supplement.
options.insight: The yearbook reports a correlation of 0.89 between People Model's AI Persona and survey results from real people. That figure measures how closely the results move together.

options.text: Drop the gift bundle and build the brand message around “I'll go myself.” Invite the mom from the interview to film the bus she usually takes.
options.feedback: After the bus video goes live, someone comments that it reminds them of their mom's bus route. You miss Friday's promo slot and the orders that came with it, and spend the weekend with the crew filming extra shots.
options.insight: The yearbook lists situations that prompt people to shop for joint supplements, including stiff knees on stairs and worrying an older relative won't be able to walk far on a family outing.

media.title: Where the Money Goes Before Nine
media.brief: The hot Americano launches next week. Manager Wu brings three printed quotes to Exit 4 at City Hall Station. There's money for one campaign, and he needs your plan by nine to get it signed off.

lines.text: Look at these. One's a monthly rate, one's priced by plays per day, and the cheapest quote is two lines long. How am I supposed to compare them?
Mr. Wu, this one counts everyone in the station. Your shop's at Exit 4, so let's pull out the traffic that actually comes this way.
Should I just buy the two busiest morning spots? My boss wants commuters to see us at least twice this week.
If both spots are on the same route, the same people might see us twice. I'll estimate reach and frequency separately.
The stores can export cup sales in half-hour blocks. Send me the ad times and I'll check the numbers each morning.
Okay, I'll add printing costs and guaranteed plays to the sheet. Which plan are we circling before we send it at nine?

steps.prompt: There's money for one campaign. Which plan do you circle on the quote sheet?

options.text: Put the budget into launch week. Book posters at Exit 4 and in the bus terminal passage to reach commuters on both routes.
options.feedback: Both routes see the new coffee in launch week, and customers send the stores photos of the posters. You spend two evenings checking the placements in person, and the month-end tally shows only a small bump in Americano sales.
options.insight: Figures from Taiwan's transport and interior ministries show total public transit ridership was 86% higher in 2017 than in 2007.

options.text: Book the Exit 4 screen from 7:30 to 9:00. Spend the rest on mobile coupons nearby and cap how often each person sees the ad.
options.feedback: The nearby store redeems more breakfast coupons, and hardly anyone uses one after nine. For days, you're checking play logs before the shop opens and chasing down each missed slot.
options.insight: Posterscope found that 83% of shoppers had seen out-of-home advertising in the 30 minutes before shopping.

options.text: Keep one small placement at Exit 4 and book a week of mobile ads. Use Friday's numbers from two stores to decide whether to spend more.
options.feedback: Both stores log morning sales on the same sheet, and the Exit 4 store is the first to show an uptick. Manager Wu reads the sheet and signs off on week two, with the other exits still off the buy.
options.insight: The 2018 yearbook identifies measurement, automated trading, and dynamic delivery as three priorities for advancing out-of-home media in Taiwan.

media.title: Do We Book the Evening Slot?
media.brief: Itch Be Gone has one reserve budget left. The quotes expire at noon, so you need to find out who will see the ads and where.

lines.text: Searches for Itch Be Gone are down. HQ wants to see orders this week.
We've got quotes for search ads and digital screens by the MRT exits. That's all the spare budget we've got.
The screen quote counts plays. Finance will kick it back if you put those in the same column as search clicks.
I'll ask the store who's buying and when they come in. Then I'll know which hours are worth pricing out.
The corner store on Songshou Road stocks it. Get back to me by noon. That's how long they'll hold the slots.

steps.hint: Songshou Rd. Corner Convenience Store: who's buying Itch Be Gone?

lines.text: Itch Be Gone? It's been raining for days. We sell the most in the after-work rush.
Are people finding the store on their phones, or are they passing by anyway?
A few regulars walk over from the MRT. They ask which aisle it's in before they've even folded their umbrellas.
Got it. Do you track sales for the morning and evening shifts separately?
Sure, I can pull that from the register. I've got the dry days too. Which dates do you want?

steps.prompt: The quotes expire at noon. How do you spend the budget?

options.text: Bid on generic search terms on rainy evenings and put the money into getting orders this week.
options.feedback: A few more online orders come in that night, but clicks on popular terms get pricier too. The budget runs out Friday, and HQ asks how many extra orders the ads actually brought in.
options.insight: After adopting data-driven attribution, E.SUN Bank found that non-brand terms accounted for nearly 60% of conversion credit. Its conversion rate rose 42% after it adjusted its campaign.

options.text: Test search ads with a small budget in one shopping district, use a similar district as a control, and hold the rest of the money.
options.feedback: You and Ah-Kai break out store sales in both districts by weather and shift, then send the numbers and ad costs to HQ. HQ agrees to wait for the next rain before increasing spend, so orders are slow to pick up this week.
options.insight: In the yearbook's nail fungus medication case, there were nearly 30% fewer rainy days than the year before. The consultant's report overlooked the local weather.

options.text: Book digital screens along the walk from the MRT exits to the store for the evening rush, with a cap on plays per loop.
options.feedback: One commuter points outside and says they just saw the same cream by the MRT exit. You and Mei split up to check the playback logs for two nights running, and sales inch up that week.
options.insight: The X-line digital out-of-home network connects more than 600 screens across Taiwan. Its total monthly traffic represents more than 100 million opportunities to see the screens.

media.title: Which Booking Goes?
media.brief: Manager Chen's lutein campaign is about to launch. There's enough money for one full schedule. Find out which placements are worth paying for.

lines.text: Look at these two quotes. Friday night's video takeover or the weekend search budget. Finance says we can keep one.
Impressions were cheap last time, but a coworker saw the same ad five times in one night. Now my boss only wants to see orders.
I'll ask the rep to hold the takeover until noon. We can split search by day, so I'd like to check when orders actually came in last year.
Go see Kai at Lanshan Plaza. He's got last year's promo orders. Take the quotes with you.

steps.hint: Go to Lanshan Plaza Data Lab and see if the client's data is usable

lines.text: Last year, most orders came in after dinner on Friday, when the add-on deal went live. See? Saturday morning is practically blank.
I'll price out search for after dinner, then. Does this video quote say how many people it'll reach?
Just impressions. Add up both platforms and you have no idea how often you've counted the same person.
Okay, I'll list cost per thousand impressions and cost per order separately. If we test by region, can you pull the orders for each one?

steps.prompt: Chen texts you that Finance is waiting. Which schedule do you send?

options.text: Drop the video takeover. Put the money into category keywords and Shopping ads after dinner on Friday.
options.feedback: Friday evening orders pick up, and Chen posts the cost per sale in the group chat. Fewer people see the new product for the first time, and the following week even the retailers ask where the ads went.
options.insight: In January 2020, Google announced it would phase out third-party cookies within two years in Chrome, which had nearly 70% market share in Taiwan.

options.text: Book one week of short-form video with a budget you can adjust daily, and save some for search. Pick comparable areas and compare orders where the ads ran with orders in the control area.
options.feedback: Orders tick up in the first week, and Chen takes the regional numbers to Finance to get the budget extended. You and Kai have to rerun the reports every day and flag the stores that ran out of stock.
options.insight: The annual report describes social and search becoming the two main gateways to media as audiences shifted from browsing to consuming content on demand.

options.text: Pass on the big takeover and split evening slots across two video platforms. Cap frequency on each platform and measure results with a brand awareness survey.
options.feedback: More people recognize the new product in the brand survey, but weekend orders drop. The platforms calculate frequency differently, and you spend several evenings with the schedule open, adjusting the next day's delivery.
options.insight: Research cited in the annual report found that 65% of Adidas sales came from brand activity. Adidas shifted its brand-to-performance budget split from 23:77 to 60:40.

media.title: Where Does the Budget Go by Four?
media.brief: Level 3 restrictions just kicked in, and the realty client wants to pull its MRT lightbox ads. Wei is waiting at the Chillshan Creative Park studio for your revised media plan for the week.

lines.text: Look, the client crossed out the MRT lightboxes. We've still got the money, but the station will only hold that 8 PM slot until four.
Let me pull up the quotes. If we put it all into prime time, there's nothing left for weekend search.
Mei-ling just texted. The branch manager still needs staff to take bookings this week. The client wants to know what number to look at once the ad runs.
For reach, I want to know how many people saw it. For bookings, I'll ask the branch to log which ones actually got confirmed.
I'll leave the 30-second master on your desk. If we're running online video, the editor can still export it today.
Got it. I'll put the frequency caps and placement rates on page four of tonight's pitch.

steps.prompt: The TV station needs an answer by four. Where do you put this week's media budget?

options.text: Release the TV hold. Buy high-intent home-viewing search terms during weekend daytime hours and send people to the booking page with the video.
options.feedback: The branch manager staffs virtual tours around the bookings and sends you the confirmed list on Monday without being asked. Most people only see the video on the booking page, and when the client asks about brand reach, you barely have a number to show.
options.insight: Citing Taiwan's National Credit Card Center, the annual report puts the online share of card transactions at 25% in January 2019 and 45% in January 2021.

options.text: Put most of the money into the 8 PM TV slot and extend reach with streaming video, capped at three views per person per week.
options.feedback: On Friday night, someone posts a photo of the TV ad taken by a family member in the branch group chat. The streaming report shows you're still reaching new viewers, but with no weekend search budget, several of the branch's virtual tour slots go unfilled.
options.insight: The annual report cites Nielsen's 2020 finding that both TV and the internet drew more attention as people spent more time at home.

options.text: Drop TV, compare the cost per thousand impressions from two video vendors, then run search in two comparable districts and add video in just one.
options.feedback: You and Ah-Kai pore over reports until midnight to remove duplicate bookings logged by the branches. The district with video reaches more people and records more valid bookings. The manager agrees to increase video spend there next week and stick to search elsewhere for now.
options.insight: Nielsen data shows that Taiwan's traditional media ad spend fell from NT$41.69 billion in 2015 to NT$25.64 billion in 2020. Over the same period, digital ad spend rose from NT$19.352 billion to NT$48.256 billion.

media.title: Where Do We Put the Budget?
media.brief: Two cases of refills are still sitting at the Shin Kong Mitsukoshi counter. Manager Hsu has NT$60,000 left for media and needs to decide today where to run ads and for how long.

lines.text: Look, we haven’t even opened these two cases of refills. I’ve got NT$60,000 left, and my boss wants results on Monday.
The rep says the screen by the elevators will play our ad 80 times a day. Is that a good deal?
That’s 80 plays. I’ll ask for weekday and weekend foot traffic so we can compare rates.
Last time all three placements shared one QR code. I could see the scans, but I couldn’t tell which screen they came from.
Let’s track them separately this time. I need to be able to explain what we paid for when I show my boss the numbers on Monday.
Sure. I’ve got quotes here for store search ads, the mall screen, and the MRT entrance screen with short videos. Let’s put the NT$60,000 behind one of them.

steps.prompt: The mall is waiting for your answer. Which buy gets the NT$60,000?

options.text: Buy weekend evening search ads on the online store. Show the refill price up front and link straight to the product page.
options.feedback: Refill orders pick up on weekend evenings. On Monday the ads come down, product page traffic drops, and searches for the brand barely move.
options.insight: In Q1 2022, Kantar surveyed 500 people in Taiwan. Of those surveyed, 85% thought eco-friendly products were more expensive.

options.text: Buy a weekday lunch slot on the mall screen and go dark at the same time the next day. Use a dedicated QR code for the product comparison page and compare counter receipts.
options.feedback: Kai goes through the receipts from both lunch slots one by one. Sales are close, though the QR code does bring some visitors to the product comparison page. Hsu uses the report to convince his boss to hold off on renewing.
options.insight: In the same Kantar survey, 71% said there wasn’t enough information about eco-friendly products.

options.text: Book the MRT entrance screen for the weekend and run short videos around the shopping district. Cap video ad impressions at two per person.
options.feedback: On Saturday afternoon, someone on Xiangti Avenue tells a friend, “That’s the refill brand from the screen at the MRT entrance.” More people ask about it at the counter, but only a few more buy. You stay until the last train two nights in a row to get the proof-of-play photos you’re missing.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that five generations have different media habits, making a single market strategy harder to pull off.

media.title: Which Slot Do We Book?
media.brief: No-Overtime Milk Tea launches a new drink tomorrow. At Lanshan Plaza, Ah-Kai spreads out the quotes and asks you where to spend the last of the media budget.

lines.text: Look at this screenshot. Someone asked what to drink after lunch in Xinyi, and the chatbot sent them next door.
I've got a quote for screens at the MRT exits. There's a lunch slot in the chatbot too. Booking both in full puts us over budget.
The chatbot placement reports clicks. We can give each placement its own coupon code and I'll match those to in-store redemptions.
I just got off the phone with the client. She wants to know how many people see the new drink. The store manager just wants to know how many extra cups he'll sell.
The screen package costs more, but it gets us the evening commute. With chat ads we can cap how often people see them or pile into lunch.
They need a signature by four thirty. Send me the media plan so I know which columns to pull tomorrow.

steps.prompt: There's only enough money to sign off on one plan. What do you book?

options.text: Put the money into evening slots at two MRT exits and run the new drink's brand ad in rotation.
options.feedback: Even commuters waiting across the street can see the new cup. You go back and forth with both vendors on the play logs until midnight. With no paid push for the lunch coupon, the store manager has a tub of ingredients left over.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that Gucci's Chengdu flagship built a three-meter-high digital mural out of 33 large LED screens.

options.text: Test one screen slot and one chat slot, cap chat frequency, and track reach and cost per redemption separately.
options.feedback: Ah-Kai puts estimated screen reach and chat impressions in separate columns and reconciles the two coupon codes. The client sees where the money went and approves another round. The small test only sells a few extra cups at lunch.
options.insight: The yearbook calls first-party data the foundation for making money with AI and points out that the quality of the input affects the output.

options.text: Put everything into lunchtime recommendations for nearby drinks, raise the frequency cap, and lead with a limited-time coupon.
options.feedback: At noon the cashier scans so many coupons the till runs out of paper. Then screenshots of one person getting the offer over and over land in the brand group chat, with jokes about it being a discount shop. The client calls to stop the ads early and wants the numbers reconciled before you clock out.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that Google and Bing have placed ads inside conversations with AI assistants, turning chat into a place to reach people with ads.

media.title: The Night Market’s 8 P.M. Slot
media.brief: One Less Piece is opening a flagship by Linginger St. Night Market. Mei-ling has two quotes, and you have until tonight to decide which hours to buy.

lines.text: One Less Piece opens next week. This quote is for the screen at the night market entrance. The other’s for mobile ads. We can’t afford both.
Eight is the priciest slot, but the quote only says how many times the ad plays. I want to see who actually looks up.
Okay. I’m putting one media plan in tonight’s pitch. The vendor’s waiting to hear about that eight o’clock slot.
I’ll walk down to the shrine on Fude Street and see which shops are still open along the way.

steps.hint: Walk the alleys to Fude St. Earth God Shrine. Note the old shops

lines.text: You were looking at the fabric shop sign, huh? They pull the shutter down at seven-thirty.
Yeah. The screen at the entrance kept playing. The only people I saw look up were waiting for fried chicken.
People heading home from work take the covered sidewalk. They’re past the shrine by six or so. The eight o’clock crowd comes for a late bite.
I’ve got both quotes open. The screen quote is for ad plays. The mobile one estimates reach and frequency.
I’ll keep those units separate. I’ll give the redemptions we can verify at the register their own column, too.

steps.prompt: You have one launch budget. Where do you spend it?

options.text: Put the budget into dinner-hour mobile ads near the night market during launch week, with an in-store discount code.
options.feedback: Codes come in at the register several nights in a row, and first-week sales jump. The budget runs out in week two, and when evening sales drop, the client asks Mei-ling why the ads only ran for one week.
options.insight: The yearbook cautions against chasing short-term traffic and results alone. Marketing investment builds up in the brand, and long-term brand strength can support short-term performance.

options.text: Split the buy between the entrance screen and backlit signs along the covered sidewalk. Run them at commute and dinner hours to reach different crowds.
options.feedback: You go back and forth with two vendors on specs and are still checking both sets of placement photos after the stalls close. Evening staff start hearing that shoppers recognized the store name on their way over, but first-week sales rise only slightly.
options.insight: The yearbook reports that UNIQLO’s East District partnership drew 2.2 times as many visitors as the year before. 91% said the store would make them visit the East District more often.

options.text: Start with a small test on two mobile placements, give each its own discount code, and move budget based on cost per redemption.
options.feedback: You and Kai spend three days matching ad invoices to register records. The placement with cheaper impressions gets fewer redemptions, so Mei-ling takes both sets of figures to the client to sign off on the shift. By the time the new buy goes live, opening weekend is over.
options.insight: The yearbook calls first-party and member data central in a world with fewer cookies. Retail media still faces fragmented data and departments working in silos.

media.title: Where the Launch Budget Goes
media.brief: The new noodles hit shelves next Monday. Ms. Su is waiting at Big Dawn Dome Broadcast Center. You need to lock in the first week's media spend tonight.

lines.text: They're waiting upstairs for your launch schedule. Procurement cleared NT$300,000. Five nights in the 8 p.m. drama slot would eat the whole thing.
The retailer's chasing us too. Their package for sponsored search and add-on placements expires tonight. Where do you want the money to go?
Can you break up the prime-time package first? I need separate rates for the noon news and the evening rerun.
The rerun costs less per spot, but some people watch both. Watch for overlap when you run the reach numbers.
Got it. I'll compare the cost per thousand impressions for the same age group, then check how many people we'd reach more than once.
Meeting upstairs in twenty. Stop by Auntie Hsiu-chin's place on Wuxing Street first. She turns on the TV when she starts prepping.

steps.hint: Wuxing St. Corner Breakfast Shop: what's everyone watching on TV?

lines.text: Auntie Hsiu-chin, is this the channel you have on when you're prepping at noon?
I watch the news at noon. The evening rerun's for people waiting on their food. See that table? They're still waiting for their egg crepes.
So you're the one watching at noon. Where do you buy noodles for the shop?
I pick up a whole case at the supermarket around the corner. The girl on the evening shift usually shops on her phone and adds stuff until shipping's free.
I'll split noon and evening on the schedule. Same TV, different people watching and buying.

steps.prompt: You've got NT$300,000 for week one. Which schedule do you take upstairs?

options.text: Put it all into sponsored search and add-on placements on the retailer's site. Run the ads only when the product's in stock.
options.feedback: Add-on orders start coming in before dinner on Monday, and the retailer sends the order report that night. The following week, hardly anyone at the supermarket asks for the new noodles, so clerks have to point them out on the shelf.
options.insight: The yearbook warns that digital ads aimed only at a target group can miss older adults who do most of the household shopping.

options.text: Buy spots in the noon news and the evening rerun, and set aside money for mobile coupon ads with a frequency cap.
options.feedback: You line up the CPMs for the same age group, and the boss signs off on both slots. In week one, shoppers show up at the supermarket with coupons on their phones, and you're checking the logs spot by spot.
options.insight: Dentsu Group estimates TV CPM at about 48 for ages 30 and up and about 247 for ages 30 to 39. YouTube CPMs typically range from 80 to 250.

options.text: Start with connected TV ads in one area, use comparable stores in another as a control, and hold the rest of the budget.
options.feedback: The boss agrees to release more money once there's a sales comparison between the two areas and puts the plan in the meeting notes. The chain-wide sales push drops off the launch schedule, and you spend every evening checking stock and sales with the stores.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that connected TV can be bought programmatically. A strong brand lift can come from reaching people who already liked the brand.

media.title: Which Slot Do We Keep?
media.brief: Outside the A25 meeting room, the MRT ad quote for a new face wash is about to expire. The budget is fixed, and Lin needs your launch-week plan before the pitch.

lines.text: That's all we've got for the face wash launch. They'll release the MRT slots at 9:10.
The client told me this afternoon they need orders to show Finance at month-end. They still want that MRT placement, too.
I just put all three quotes on a cost-per-thousand basis. If I sign for the MRT package, I'll have to cut the evening shopping ads.
Last time the short videos ran seven times per person on average, and reach still stalled. More money might just buy more of the same audience.
I'll put a frequency cap in the plan. Ah-Kai, can we hold back one group from the video ads? I want to see how many extra orders we get.
The client's inside. Page nine gets one media schedule. You make the call.

steps.prompt: The launch-week budget covers one plan. Which schedule do you take into the room?

options.text: Put most of the money into evening on-site search and product-page ads to reach people ready to buy.
options.feedback: Evening orders pick up, and Mei posts the numbers in the client chat the next day. At month-end, the client sees that many shoppers were already searching for the brand and asks how many extra orders the spend actually brought in.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that on a per-thousand-impressions basis, placements billed per click often cost five to ten times as much as CPM placements or more. Attention quality and incremental impact matter too.

options.text: Keep a small on-site search buy. Spend the rest on two waves of short video, cap frequency, and keep one group out of the video buy for comparison.
options.feedback: You and Ah-Kai stay at A25 splitting the audience lists and checking orders until your boxed dinners go cold. The first wave shows the client how many extra orders came in, and they agree to shift the second wave's spend to placements where reach is still growing.
options.insight: The yearbook distinguishes attribution from incrementality and points out that clients with urgent questions often can't wait weeks for a study.
