options.text: Drop launch-week shopping ads and book the screens at Taipei City Hall MRT station for the evening commute so the new product shows up on the way home.
options.feedback: You check every screen with the vendor before the last train, and the client gets a commuter's Story the next morning. People start asking about the product, but launch-week orders come in below forecast.
options.insight: The yearbook cites CeraVe's MRT campaign with sample bottles on the hand straps, which sparked 24,000 posts in a single day.

creative.title: Before the Doors Close
creative.brief: The hot Americano launches next week. Manager Wu brings the rejected ad proof to City Hall Station and asks you to find an image that will make commuters look up.

lines.text: Good timing. I printed the proof. Everything circled in red is something my boss wants bigger.
Try looking from the far end of the escalator. Can you make out anything besides the price?
All I can see of the cup is a sliver of white. But a few people just looked up when they heard the doors closing.
I saw your sketch. Can you really make the train doors turn into a coffee cup as they close?
I'll shoot a test with a paper cup and two gray boards. If we lead with the deal, I'll cut a separate version.
We can only greenlight one today. Show me what you've got and I'll take it to my boss this afternoon.

steps.prompt: Print and video both need final artwork today. Which version do you make first?

options.text: Shoot a six-second spot where closing train doors turn into a paper cup. Reveal the brand in the final second and leave the price for the store.
options.feedback: You and the editor work past midnight to line up the gap between the doors with the cup. The next day, people on Facebook ask which coffee chain made the ad, while the stores sell only a few extra cups.
options.insight: The yearbook says total public transit ridership in Taiwan rose 86% from 2007 to 2017. Measurement remains a challenge for out-of-home advertising in Taiwan.

options.text: Open with the hot Americano and the breakfast add-on price. Shoot a close-up of a barista handing over the cup, then end with directions to the store.
options.feedback: A barista helps you get the extra shot before their shift, and you recut the spot twice before it goes live. The next day, more customers add coffee to breakfast, and one remembers the deal but still has to ask which chain is running it.
options.insight: Posterscope found that 83% of shoppers saw an out-of-home ad in the 30 minutes before shopping.

options.text: Make a station poster with the cup photo you already have and a matching sign for the store. Walk the route with Manager Wu and the proofs, then pilot the offer at one store.
options.feedback: At the exit, Manager Wu realizes the arrow sends people across the street and asks you to fix it on the spot. When a customer points at the sign and adds a coffee during the trial, he takes the revised proof to his boss for sign-off.
options.insight: In its discussion of omnichannel experiences, the yearbook recommends mapping the customer journey to find where it breaks down, then starting with a small, workable pilot.

creative.title: Do We Cut the Shot with the Boots?
creative.brief: The Itch Be Gone ad goes live tomorrow. HQ just axed the studio shoot and wants a product shot where the rain boots used to be.

lines.text: Searches for Itch Be Gone are down. HQ wants the tube on screen in the first second.
The studio shoot's gone, too. They need a cut by noon or they'll run last year's.
I remember those boots you drew. Will people know where to buy the stuff, though?
I'll go take a look. The store might have the shot we're missing.
Try the corner store on Songshou Road. While you're there, ask who's been buying lately.

steps.hint: Songshou Rd. Corner Convenience Store: who's buying Itch Be Gone?

lines.text: A delivery guy came in this morning, stood by that red chair, and poured water out of his rain boots.
Did he grab the cream right after that?
He stuffed his wet socks into one of our plastic bags first. Then he came over and asked where we kept the cream.
We could keep the bit where he ties the bag. Which shelf is it on? Mind if I get a shot?
Second shelf to the right of the register. You can shoot the shelf, just keep customers' faces out of frame.

steps.prompt: You've got a shelf photo on your phone and time to send one cut before lunch. What do you do?

options.text: Cut a six-second sales spot from the existing product shots and show where to find it by the register.
options.feedback: The spot makes the next day's slot. The clerk says someone came in with the ad on their phone and bought a tube on the spot. Then HQ hears from other stores: they don't stock it by the register.
options.insight: The 2019 yearbook notes that E.SUN Bank used data-driven attribution and found that non-brand keywords accounted for nearly 60% of conversion credit. After adjustments, its conversion rate rose 42%.

options.text: Make two storyboard cuts on your phone and ask Kai to show them to a few people and see if they can point out where the cream is stocked.
options.feedback: A few people who see the boots-first cut recognize the box but miss where the register is. You send HQ the results and both cuts, and they give you half a day to pick up a shelf shot.
options.insight: The 2019 yearbook points out that data only covers what gets recorded. Sample surveys, interviews at stores, and small data can help uncover clues it misses.

options.text: Borrow the store for the last half hour before closing and shoot a short film following a delivery rider from emptying his boots to buying the cream.
options.feedback: You kneel in the doorway to reshoot the water pouring out, then edit back at the office until the last train's gone. The film goes up a day late, but someone in the comments recognizes their own kind of rain boots and tags the brand for a coworker to see.
options.insight: The 2019 yearbook discusses weaving brands into stories as a way to reach people who skip or block ads. It also stresses that the placement has to serve the story.

creative.title: The Shot Outside the Pharmacy
creative.brief: The health supplement ad loses its studio budget before filming. Manager Chen has a noon presentation, and on your way to Lanshan Plaza you need to decide whether to keep the shot outside the pharmacy.

lines.text: When the pandemic hit, my boss cut the studio budget. He wants that money spent on traffic, but he still wants to see a new cut at noon.
That woman at the start opens her paper bag outside the pharmacy. My boss wants to know why our bottle isn't on screen in the first second.
She's digging out the bottle she bought by mistake last time. It's that crumpled receipt I want to keep in the shot.
Last year's orders and the stores' customer inquiries are at Lanshan Plaza. Can you take a look? I need to know if that scene is worth filming.

steps.hint: Go to Lanshan Plaza Data Lab and see if the client's data is usable

lines.text: The orders tell us what sold. For questions, you need the shift log. Here's one: a customer brought in an empty bottle to ask if it was the same product.
We can shoot that. Phone right up by the counter, hands and the empty bottle in frame, clerk answering through a mask. Saves us the rental, too.
Sure. Chen still needs one slide for noon that tells his boss how we'll judge whether the ad worked.

steps.prompt: Ten minutes to noon. Which cut goes into Manager Chen's deck?

options.text: Cut a six-second sales spot. Put the bottle, discount, and buy button in the first frame.
options.feedback: The stock product photo goes live that afternoon, and the discounted bundles sell out fast. Chen sends a screenshot of someone posting a rival's bottle and asking if it’s part of the same deal.
options.insight: A survey cited in the yearbook found that 73% use their phones while eating and 71% do so while watching TV.

options.text: Film the clerk answering the empty-bottle question. Have Chen sign off on the captions and link to the product page at the end.
options.feedback: Chen asks the store team to check the captions, and the video goes live after two rounds of edits. Orders start coming in from viewers who clicked through, and Chen gives customer support the same cut to use in replies.
options.insight: In a Salesforce survey cited in the yearbook, 84% of customers said content, interactions, and service at each touchpoint were as important as the product itself.

options.text: Keep the shot outside the pharmacy, build three short films around it, and run them on the brand budget first.
options.feedback: You shoot inserts of the hands on your phone and spend two nights cutting the three films together. Someone in the comments recognizes the crumpled bag, but the promotion gets fewer placements and orders are down this week.
options.insight: The yearbook cites third-party research finding that 65% of Adidas sales came from brand campaigns. Adidas later shifted its brand-to-performance budget from 23:77 to 60:40.

creative.title: Under the Door
creative.brief: Level 3 restrictions have knocked out the realty shoot's location. There's one door on the Chillshan Creative Park soundstage, and the spot for tonight's pitch has to be in the can by four.

lines.text: We lost the location. Art built us this door. Pan an inch to the right and you'll see the set ends.
The client just messaged me on LINE. Can people book a virtual viewing straight from the ad?
Wei, look at this take. The kid slips her drawing under the door and her dad crouches to pick it up.
I like that shot. The client circled it and wrote 'cut.' Says they can't tell who we're helping find a home.
She drew the room she wants. I want to hold on her dad for a beat while he unfolds it.
Okay. We're out of here at four. Tell the camera crew what you want to shoot next.

steps.prompt: You've got a door and a phone. How do you shoot these thirty seconds?

options.text: Shoot a virtual viewing demo. Use the phone screen to show the light and layout, then put a booking link on the end card.
options.feedback: The client sees it on the monitor and signs off, and you wrap before four. Bookings come in from the end card, and the agents repost just the bit that shows how to use the phone.
options.insight: The yearbook identified Home Commerce as an opportunity during the pandemic and noted that consumers had higher expectations for how they interact with brands.

options.text: Keep the shot under the door. Open on the sound of paper scraping against it, then hold the branding until Dad unfolds the drawing and we see the window his daughter drew.
options.feedback: You spend take after take flat on the floor with the camera operator until you catch that little pause as Dad reaches down. People share the shot of the crooked window, while the sales team reports few bookings from the spot.
options.insight: Sinyi Realty's “Trust and Happiness” deliberately left the sales pitch out. In post-testing, 70% of viewers shifted in a positive direction, compared with a previous KPI of 20 to 30%.

options.text: Keep the door scene and pick up a vertical close-up of the phone. Let the father and daughter scene play out in widescreen, and cut from the drawing to the booking screen in the vertical version.
options.feedback: You get the last shot before four, then stay with the editor until midnight to line up the paper sound with the cut to the phone. The widescreen cut gets shared and the vertical cut brings in bookings. The client schedules both for release.
options.insight: The yearbook cautions against taking what you observe in the data at face value.

creative.title: Don't Toss That Bottle Yet
creative.brief: At the Shin Kong Mitsukoshi cleaning products counter, Manager Hsu sends your refill ad back for changes. You've got half a day left in the studio to rethink the opening shot.

lines.text: I'm holding this cut. Eight seconds of floating leaves and I still don't know how to use the pouch.
A shopper just picked up the refill, then put the original bottle back. She wasn't sure the two would fit.
That's why I wanted a shot that actually shows the pour. But my boss wants the price in the first three seconds.
Half a day left in the studio. Pull the fake grass off the set. Keep the sink.
One more thing. I can't sign off on 'zero impact on the planet.' That part needs a recut.
All right, I'll sketch the opening. What do we want her to see before she scrolls past?

steps.prompt: You've got half a day left in the studio. What goes in the opening shot?

options.text: Open with the in-store deal, then cut to close-ups of tearing the pouch open and pouring it into the original bottle.
options.feedback: Over the weekend, shoppers pull up the video at the counter and buy the refill. Once the deal ends, even the counter staff only remember that red price card at the start.
options.insight: In a Kantar survey of 500 people in Taiwan, 85% thought eco-friendly products cost more.

options.text: Film the refill in one continuous take and end with usage figures the client can back up.
options.feedback: You move the lights three times to get the bottle markings to show. Manager Hsu gets the same cut approved and leaves it with the counter staff for demos, though weekend sales barely budge.
options.insight: In the Kantar survey, 71% of respondents felt there wasn't enough information about eco-friendly products.

options.text: Show the empty bottle nearly getting tossed, then use match cuts to bring it back to the sink and fill it again and again.
options.feedback: Someone posts a photo of the same bottle, worn and faded, and others shoot their own versions. Refills move a little slower, and you stay late cutting a vertical edit where a hand one frame out of place ruins the match.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that Facebook reduced Pages' organic reach in the fourth quarter of 2017. Relevance, value, and an emotional response can help content get seen.

creative.title: The Sound of Clocking Out
creative.brief: The new milk tea goes on sale at 8 tomorrow morning. The client saw the AI storyboard for the vertical spot and wants the time clock cut from the opening.

lines.text: I played the rough cut on my phone here in the data lab. Two seconds of a time clock, and the client asked if we were hiring.
Wait for the click. The time card pops out, then the straw punches through the cup seal. I want you to hear it and know the shift is over.
The client wants the cup and the promo code right up front. We can move money out of print, but we only get an hour in the shop after closing.
That cup in the storyboard has milk foam the shop doesn’t serve. I’ll get you a time clock. We’ll have to reshoot the cup.
I’ll shoot a close-up with the real cup on the desk first. Once I cut those two shots together, the client can see what I’m going for.
Okay, I’ll set up the phone. We need a vertical cut by eight tomorrow morning. How do you want to edit it?

steps.prompt: You have one hour in the shop. How do you make the spot that goes live at 8 tomorrow morning?

options.text: Shoot in the shop. Cut from the time clock click to the straw piercing the seal, and put the offer on a separate graphic.
options.feedback: You and the editor work till the small hours to get the sounds to line up. A shop employee even does the click when they share the clip, but the offer is on a separate graphic and few morning orders come through the video.
options.insight: The yearbook says even people with no art training can sketch with prompts. It still takes a person to judge how an image feels and whether it’s usable.

options.text: Shoot the real cup and make two cuts from the same footage. Give the client a story-first cut and a product-first cut to watch side by side tonight.
options.feedback: The client keeps the clock sound, agrees to move the real cup up to the first second, and signs off on keeping the AI images in the pitch deck. You and the editor make an extra cut, and the shop crew is already prepping ingredients by the time it’s locked.
options.insight: The yearbook warns that misleading content and infringement can seriously hurt a brand. It recommends putting AI disclosure clauses in contracts.

options.text: Lead with the promo code and keep the cup from the AI storyboard to catch the breakfast crowd.
options.feedback: Commuters scan the code to order, and morning orders beat the forecast. Someone posts a screenshot asking where the milk foam is, so the shop manager calls for a replacement and you have to reshoot and export the spot again.
options.insight: The yearbook points out that generated content is getting cheaper while verification costs are rising. What once took a second to verify can now take a minute, ten minutes, or even an hour.

creative.title: Pass the Hanger
creative.brief: The launch video for One Less Piece just got sent back. Mei-ling needs a storyboard you can actually shoot before tonight's pitch.

lines.text: One Less Piece opens its flagship on Linginger Street next week. The client just sent the launch video back.
The AI mock-up? By the third glowing hanger, I was ready to swipe.
I wanted to cut that hanger too. Which shot did the client keep?
Just the store name at the end. They want it vertical, and we've got half a day to shoot.
I'll take my phone down to the Earth God shrine on Fude Street. Wei, can you grab the storyboard?

steps.hint: Walk the alleys to Fude St. Earth God Shrine. Note the old shops

lines.text: Miss, could you move that tripod? The fabric shop owner needs to get his cart through.
Wait, he just handed the jacket, hanger and all, to the guy next door to try on. Mind if I ask him to do it again?
Go ahead. Show him what you shoot, though. He's worried people will only remember the flagship.
I want to open on his hand. Then we cut to someone taking the jacket at the next shop's door.
That could work. In half a day, we'll need the shops to stick to our schedule. And the client still wants to know if the price can go in the first second.

steps.prompt: Mei-ling's waiting for the storyboard. What do you shoot with half a day?

options.text: Shoot a try-on ad. Put the launch price in the first second and the shopping link at the end.
options.feedback: The clerk changes outfits three times outside the fitting room, and it takes one last take to get the cuff in focus. Orders come in as soon as the launch price goes live. You cut the fabric shop owner's cameo, and when he sees the ad, he asks you to take his shop's name out too.
options.insight: The 2024 report lists short-form video and livestream shopping as social media trends. It also warns brands against chasing only short-term traffic and results.

options.text: Shoot a relay through the neighborhood, passing the jacket from the fabric shop all the way to the flagship.
options.feedback: The fabric cart arrives late, and you crouch under the arcade and reshoot seven times before the hands match across the cut. When the video goes live, people recognize the fabric shop owner and tag One Less Piece when they share it. The comments are full of people naming shops, with few asking about the price.
options.insight: In the report's UNIQLO East District case, the neighborhood collaboration hit 105% of its sales target and drew 2.2 times the previous year's visitors.

options.text: Film a clerk's demo with large type for sizes, the launch price, and how to try things on.
options.feedback: Mei-ling checks every title card with the store manager, and the client signs off on the cut that night. At the opening, a shopper points to the jacket on the screen by the door and asks for it in their size. Without the neighborhood sequence, the clip gets few shares.
options.insight: In its discussion of shopping across channels, the 2024 report reminds brands to consider older customers and people with established shopping habits.

creative.title: A Seat at the Table
creative.brief: Su is waiting for you at the broadcast center to lock the shooting script. The soy sauce spot shoots tomorrow, and the client just crossed out the best shot on your storyboard.

lines.text: The client crossed out the shot where she pulls out the chair. He's worried people will scroll past if the first three seconds feel empty.
He wants the soy sauce bottle in the first second. He even asked if we could slap the discount on the label.
That chair's for the daughter getting off work late. When she sits, you finally get why there's an extra bowl of rice.
Camera crew's in at seven tomorrow. We've got the table and lights for one day. You need to call the shots tonight.
Go see Auntie Xiuqin on the corner. She usually mutes the TV. See what you can still follow with the sound off.

steps.hint: Wuxing St. Corner Breakfast Shop: what's everyone watching on TV?

lines.text: I muted the TV so I could hear the orders. Hey, leave that chair there for now.
Is someone else joining them?
Yeah, her daughter's just finishing her shift across the street. Look, she's even unwrapped the chopsticks for her.
Those unwrapped chopsticks tell you someone's waiting for her. I want that in the shot.
Sure. Eat up first, though. Once that egg pancake goes cold, I can't give you another take.

steps.prompt: You've got one day to shoot. Which shot list are you handing in?

options.text: Open on a vertical close-up of the pour. Get the deal and store link in before six seconds.
options.feedback: The client signs off that night. Once the clip goes live, the store sells out of the promo bundle. In follow-ups, some people remember the discount but can't name the soy sauce brand.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that Reels accounts for 50% of time spent on Instagram.

options.text: Keep the chair scene. Show the family waiting in the TV spot and open on the unwrapped chopsticks in the vertical cut.
options.feedback: The crew relights for two framings, and their dinner's cold by wrap. After it airs, viewers post photos of the bowls they set aside at home and tag the soy sauce brand. The store link at the end of the vertical cut brings in orders too.
options.insight: The yearbook calls for content that feels native to each screen while keeping the brand consistent.

options.text: Shoot two phone tests, one opening on the rice bowl and one on the bottle. Show them to people who haven't bought the brand.
options.feedback: You and Wei stay up past midnight editing, and the client joins the screening the next day. Someone mentions the chopsticks after the rice bowl cut, so the client agrees to keep the scene. The launch slips past the store promotion.
options.insight: The yearbook warns that brand lift may only reflect people who already support the brand, and algorithms favor serving ads to the easiest people to reach.

creative.title: The Buckle Click
creative.brief: Just before the pitch, the retailer pulls the commuter bag ad. Its AI-cut opening looks almost identical to a rival's. Lin wants you to pick the cut for slide nine.

lines.text: Buy First Select just pulled the ad. They put ours next to the rival's. Both open with someone crossing the street in the rain.
They cut the location shoot. Tonight's promo code is still on. Marketing wants orders from the opening shot, and the product team wants final approval.
Look at this frame. The editing agent says this shot will sell. It even swapped the buckle for a silver one.
The real one's black. I shot a try-on on Wuxing Street today. A woman clips the strap and frees up a hand to grab her breakfast.
I ran both cuts through a simulated audience. It helped pick an opener. We'll need real viewers to see if they'd buy.
They're waiting in the conference room. You're the creative. Which cut goes on slide nine? Tell me what can go straight out and what needs a sign-off.

steps.prompt: The client cut the location shoot. The room's waiting for one rough cut. What's going on slide nine?

options.text: Make tonight's slot with the AI cut. Put the promo code in the first second and let the agent pick the opener and publish.
options.feedback: The promo code brings in a rush of orders. The next day, the product team gets a string of comments asking about the silver buckle, and the client asks to revoke the agent's publishing access.
options.insight: The annual report lists four levels of agent permissions: observe and understand, recommend, decide, and act.

options.text: Shoot the real black buckle at A25. Keep the offer at the end and get the product team to sign off on every format before it goes live.
options.feedback: You and Mei are still shooting at A25 when security comes through on rounds. The product team clears each cut, and the offer goes live just before the promo ends.
options.insight: The annual report describes four steps for keeping mass-produced content from all looking alike: set specs, build a production line, inspect the work, and turn what works into repeatable patterns.

options.text: Pull tonight's promo cut. Make a short from the Wuxing Street footage with the location audio, starting with the click of the buckle.
options.feedback: Without the promo cut driving sales, fewer orders come in that night. You stay at the edit desk past midnight replaying the buckle click. The next day, the client makes it the opener for the series, and people start asking where the bag's from.
options.insight: The annual report notes that Coinbase had real actors play video game NPCs and kept the imperfections in their performances so people could tell it was made by humans.

data.title: Does That Cup Count?
data.brief: The hot Americano launches next week. Manager Wu spreads the trial sales report out at MRT City Hall Station. She wants to know how many extra cups a station ad could sell.

lines.text: Look, more people came out of the station on the trial day, and hot Americanos sold well. My boss says we should book this wall.
This column counts exits across the whole station. That whole crowd just took the turn toward the bus terminal without passing this wall.
Our stores were also handing out coupons at the register. How do I tell what brought people in?
I just checked the receipts. There's a refunded cup still in the sales total. Hold off on that screenshot.
I'll take out the refunds. If we're looking for extra sales from the ad, I'd like some time slots without it to compare against.
We've got a month's budget. I have to head back to the office soon. Pick an approach and tell me what I can take to my boss at the end of the month.

steps.prompt: The City Hall Station budget covers one plan. What evidence will you bring back at the end of the month?

options.text: Take the whole bus terminal passage wall. Before and after it goes up, stop commuters at the same exit and ask which coffee brands they remember.
options.feedback: By month's end, more people name the brand without a list of choices, and Manager Wu puts the chart on her first slide. You spend three mornings at the exit collecting extra responses, and the 'extra cups sold' cell in Finance's sheet is still blank.
options.insight: The yearbook cites Dentsu Japan research finding that out-of-home plus mobile ads got 2.2 times the ad recall of mobile alone.

options.text: Pair similar morning slots and draw lots to decide which runs the coffee ad and which shows station directions. Compare sales at nearby stores.
options.feedback: Stores sell a few more hot Americanos in the half hour after the ad than after the station directions, so Manager Wu spends the rest of the budget on morning slots. You still have to reconcile the playback logs slot by slot. One day the screen starts late, and you flag that slot in the report.
options.insight: The yearbook identifies measurement, automated trading, and dynamic delivery as three keys to developing Taiwan's out-of-home media.

options.text: Put a station-specific discount code on one small board. Ask the stores for a weekly export of redemption receipts and match them against the register data.
options.feedback: The store manager finds a refunded sale in the receipts, and Manager Wu crosses it off the redemption sheet with you. She keeps the discount running the following week and tells her boss how many redemptions went through.
options.insight: The yearbook cites Posterscope research finding that 83% of shoppers saw an out-of-home ad within 30 minutes before shopping.

data.title: Three Zeros in the Spreadsheet
data.brief: HQ points to a search chart and says Itch Be Gone isn't selling. Lin wants you to trace the numbers and decide where the extra ad budget should go.

lines.text: HQ dropped this red line into a slide called "Sales Are Down." Can you tell me where this column came from?
It's an export from a search tool. I got the raw file from the vendor. There's not a single receipt in it.
I've got the store's sales, but it shows zero from Wednesday through Friday last week. I want to see the delivery records for those days.
Ask at the store on Songshou Road. Get back to me by eleven thirty. HQ's waiting to release the budget.

steps.hint: Songshou Rd. Corner Convenience Store: who's buying Itch Be Gone?

lines.text: I'm checking sales for Itch Be Gone. Do you have last Friday's delivery slip?
Hang on. We sold out Tuesday, and the next shipment came Saturday. Look, the date's right under the barcode.
That explains three days without a single sale. Who was buying on Tuesday?
One older guy was out making deliveries on his scooter. His raincoat was still dripping. He asked for the same tube as last time. Even remembered the color of the box.
And that sale never shows up in the search report. Let me mark those three days as out of stock.

steps.prompt: HQ will release one round of funding for now. Where do you spend it, and what numbers will you bring back?

options.text: Bid on branded searches where stores have stock, and track orders with a dedicated promo code.
options.feedback: Stores with stock start seeing promo codes at the register, and weekend sales beat last week's. Finance checks the loyalty records, spots several repeat buyers, and asks you to work out how much new business the ads actually brought in.
options.insight: After adopting data-driven attribution, E.SUN Bank found that nearly 60% of conversion credit went to non-brand keywords.

options.text: Pair in-stock shopping areas with similar rainfall, then randomly boost ads in one area per pair and keep the other's budget steady.
options.feedback: You and Ah-Kai check inventory and register data every day. The report takes until the following week. Sales rise in both areas when it rains, and extra ads barely widen the gap, so Lin uses the two sales reports to put a stop to the blanket increase.
options.insight: In the yearbook's nail fungus treatment case, there were nearly 30% fewer rainy days than the year before.

options.text: Listen to what shoppers ask for in stores, then test which of two shelf signs helps people remember the brand name.
options.feedback: You and a coworker take turns by the register and catch the evening crowd too. More shoppers remember the name when it's printed larger, so the client asks stores to swap the signs and check sales at the end of the month.
options.insight: The yearbook recommends pairing big data with sample surveys, retail interviews, and small data to catch what existing records miss.

data.title: Who Gets Credit for This Order?
data.brief: The supplement brand’s ad report is full of green arrows. Finance wants to know where the money is. Before the noon meeting, Chen asks you, the data analyst, to take a look.

lines.text: It’s freezing in this meeting room at Taipei 101. Keep your jacket on and take a look at these two printouts.
We started sending shoppers to our site during the pandemic. Ads and LINE both show sales, but finance barely sees any extra orders.
You’ve circled 0317 on both pages. Can I get the full order numbers? I want to see if it’s the same purchase.
Last year’s order file is at the Lanshan Plaza data lab. I’ll ask Kai to pull up this month’s payments too.
All right. Hold that slide for the noon meeting. Kai and I will match the orders and get back to you.

steps.hint: Go to Lanshan Plaza Data Lab and see if the client's data is usable

lines.text: Full order number matches for 0317. The customer clicked an ad, then opened LINE for a coupon before checking out.
So both reports claimed the same order. What about the one in orange?
Refunded. Still in the ad report, though. I found the same thing in last year’s file.
Right, I’m crossing out “extra orders from ads.” At noon, we need to tell them what we’ll measure next.

steps.prompt: Ten minutes to noon. Chen needs you to pick one approach. What do you go with?

options.text: A/B test a checkout coupon. Pick the winner on net revenue and pause ads aimed at new customers.
options.feedback: The coupon group still brings in more revenue after refunds, so Chen rolls it out that week. The social media editor comes over to ask if there’s any budget left for the video meant to bring in new customers.
options.insight: The yearbook describes tests by Amnet in which machine-learning ad delivery brought average CPA down by roughly 50% or more compared with standard tactics.

options.text: Reconcile orders with finance. Remove duplicates and refunds, then send a weekly report anyone can reproduce.
options.feedback: Finance runs the numbers on the same file and finally gets the same total you do. Chen uses the report to approve a restock, but it’ll take a separate experiment to see how many extra sales the ads drove.
options.insight: The yearbook cites an early 2019 survey by Vicki Boykis in which data specialists spent 67% of their time cleaning and organizing data.

options.text: Move some promo money into brand ads. Pair similar regions and randomly pick one from each pair to run the ads, then measure brand awareness.
options.feedback: You and Kai work late checking the ad delivery logs and surveys for each region. Brand awareness rises more where the ads run than in the control regions, but with fewer promos you sell a few fewer cases this quarter.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that a third-party study attributed 65% of Adidas sales to brand campaigns. Adidas then shifted its brand-to-performance budget to 60:40.

data.title: What Drove That Green Line?
data.brief: The Chillshan Creative Park studio closes at four. A realty client is pushing Wei to sign off on the strength of a teaser click chart. It is up to the data analyst to check whether those clicks led to bookings.

lines.text: You work with data. Take a look at this chart for me? The realty team says the green line is up and wants it in tonight’s pitch.
They want a booking button at the end of the main spot. They say that button is what got people to book viewings off the teaser.
I pulled the raw export. That green line counts form opens. If I open it three times, that’s three hits.
The branch sheet only has confirmed bookings. There’s no source column, so we can’t match the two.
The client’s here at four to pick up the cut. What do I put on the slide in place of “The ad drove bookings”?
We’ll shoot the spot as planned. You tell me what goes on the end card and what goes on tonight’s slide.

steps.prompt: The end card is due at four. Which result do you measure first?

options.text: Keep the booking button and use a dedicated link to match submissions to confirmed bookings.
options.feedback: The branch removes duplicates by booking ID and schedules viewings that week. The client signs off on the weekly report, but shares lag.
options.insight: The yearbook says that as third-party cookies go away, brands need to build up their own first-party data and identity systems.

options.text: Give the brand the end card and measure recall against a group that hasn’t seen the spot.
options.feedback: The editor barely gets the brand card in before launch. The survey comes back the next day, and more people in the viewing group can name the realty firm unaided. Sales still can’t find any bookings they can trace to the spot.
options.insight: In the post-test for Sinyi Realty’s “Trust and Happiness,” 70% of viewers showed a positive shift, compared with the previous KPI of 20 to 30%.

options.text: Randomly split viewers between two end cards for the same spot and compare bookings and brand recall.
options.feedback: You and Kai work past midnight to clear out duplicate submissions. The button gets more confirmed bookings and the brand card gets better recall. The client runs the brand cut as the main spot and keeps the button cut for driving bookings.
options.insight: The yearbook warns against taking patterns in search or other data at face value.

data.title: The Stack of Returns
data.brief: Refill sales jump in the Shin Kong Mitsukoshi anniversary sale report. Manager Hsu slides a stack of return slips across the counter and asks you how much they really sold.

lines.text: Could you take a look at this? The chart shoots up on Saturday, but the counter staff say there’s still a whole case they never opened.
I checked the register logs. Returns have their own transaction code, and this report only pulls sales.
I took out the returns. Saturday still comes out on top. That’s when we sent out coupons and had someone at the counter showing people how to pour the refills.
Right, we did both on Saturday. My boss saw the numbers and asked me to print another batch of coupons for next week.
Hang on. Let’s test one thing first. If we run both again, we’ll still be guessing.
Okay, the counter staff can help with one round. At Friday’s meeting, I need you to tell me if this is worth paying for.

steps.prompt: Manager Hsu can fit in one round of testing. What do you check first?

options.text: Randomly give half the members a refill coupon, then compare purchase rates after accounting for returns.
options.feedback: More members bought refills in the coupon group, so Manager Hsu ordered another case. The following week, a shopper asked when the next coupons were coming and put the refill back on the shelf.
options.insight: In the first quarter of 2022, Kantar surveyed 500 people in Taiwan. Some 85% thought eco-friendly products cost more, and 76% cited convenience and cost as reasons for not taking action.

options.text: Weigh the empty bottle and pouch, put the figures on a card, and randomly show it to half the shoppers. Track sales and follow-up questions.
options.feedback: You borrowed a digital scale, worked out the difference in packaging weight for the same volume, and left the weighing log at the counter. When a shopper came back with the card to ask if the cap was included, Manager Hsu opened the log and answered on the spot.
options.insight: In the same Kantar survey, 71% of respondents felt they had too little information.

options.text: Hold public demos using empty bottles of the same kind. Randomly assign demos to comparable time slots and compare stops and QR-code shares with and without a demo.
options.feedback: Several shoppers tried pouring the refill, scanned the display code, and sent the brand’s how-to page to friends. Sales were only up a few units, and you and the staff were still washing measuring cups in the back after the demo.
options.insight: The yearbook features IKEA’s secondhand market as a sustainability case study.

data.title: Where Did Those Extra Orders Come From?
data.brief: At Lanshan Plaza, the dashboard shows a 30% jump in milk tea orders after the AI ordering assistant went live. Ah-Kai asks you to check the payments. The client needs a decision by 5 p.m. for tomorrow's 8 a.m. launch.

lines.text: Hey, take a look. No-Overtime Milk Tea tried AI ordering, and the dashboard says orders are up 30%.
The client already made a graphic to celebrate. They need an answer by 5 p.m.. Do we turn the assistant on at every store for the eight o'clock launch tomorrow?
I checked the payment export. Same order number. Each retry adds a row, but the customer only gets charged once.
No wonder the stores didn't cook any extra pearls. We sent out an NT$10 coupon during yesterday's pilot, too. Nobody kept a control group.
If we want to see how many drinks the AI actually sells, give both groups the same coupon and put one on the regular menu. Then count paid orders.
The store manager just texted. They're out of taro balls and the assistant is still pushing them. I need to settle tomorrow's ordering setup with the client.

steps.prompt: The client is waiting in the group chat. How will customers order the new drink tomorrow morning?

options.text: Turn off the assistant and the coupon. Check what's in stock with the stores and post a menu people can share.
options.feedback: You call every store and pull sold-out toppings from the menu graphic. It's nearly midnight by the time you're done. Regulars share it in local groups and the brand page gets more comments, but without the coupon, launch-day orders come in below expectations.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that conversational search can fall behind on updates and even recommend restaurants that have already closed.

options.text: Give both groups the same coupon, randomly send customers to the AI assistant or the regular menu, and compare paid orders.
options.feedback: You and Ah-Kai check the payments, and the two groups have about the same paid conversion rate, with coupon redemptions in both. The client pulls the celebration graphic and asks for another update next week. Half the traffic stays on the regular menu as a control this week, so the assistant rollout stays on hold.
options.insight: The yearbook calls first-party data the foundation for making money with AI. Poor data in means poor results out.

options.text: Turn on the assistant at every store, send the coupon as planned, and track launch-day paid orders in the payment records.
options.feedback: The coupons go out and paid orders do rise that day. The assistant keeps pushing sold-out taro balls, so customers post the chats in local groups, and you and Mei-ling scramble to fix orders and refund the difference. The client asks how many extra orders the assistant drove, and all you have is the chain-wide total.
options.insight: Citing Similarweb's 2023 figures, the yearbook reports that visits to Bing rose by 15% at one point after it integrated ChatGPT.

data.title: One Phone, Two Visitors
data.brief: The flagship opens next week. Mei hands you the soft-opening report and asks whether those night-market scans turned into sales.

lines.text: One Less Piece opens next week. The client saw the soft-opening report and thinks everyone on Linginger Street came in to buy clothes.
They want that slide tonight. Can you check what they're counting as a visitor?
That column's from GA4. Kai, did we get the register export too?
Yep. The front door and the alley have the same QR code, and the report counts every page open.
I'll scan one along the way and another at the Earth God shrine on Fude Street. Keep an eye on the live report.

steps.hint: Walk the alleys to Fude St. Earth God Shrine. Note the old shops

lines.text: The shrine sticker's on the back of a red chair. I just scanned it on the same phone. Did it show up?
Yep, two page opens. Nothing new on the register, and you're still at the shrine.
I'll change 'new visitors' to 'page opens' on the slide. The growth chart can come out for now.
Okay, I'll talk to the client. We've got one opening budget. What do you want to measure first?

steps.prompt: There's room for one measurement plan. Which number do you want to pin down first?

options.text: Randomly offer express checkout and compare purchases at the register. Keep opening staff at the flagship.
options.feedback: The group offered express checkout is more likely to pay, so the manager opens another express register the next day. The shaved-ice shop owner sees the line blocking his door and tells you to find somewhere else for your posters next time.
options.insight: The 2024 report cautions against chasing short-term traffic and performance alone. Brand is where all those marketing investments add up.

options.text: Randomly assign poster slots at local shops. Ask people on the street which brands they remember when the posters are up and when they're down.
options.feedback: It takes you and Mei several trips to get the shops on a rotation. More people can name the store without a prompt during poster slots, but when the manager asks how many more clothes he sold, you don't have an answer yet.
options.insight: UNIQLO's East District program drew 2.2 times as many visitors as the year before. 91% said the store would bring them to the area more often.

options.text: Reconcile the register data with the client, randomly offer a coupon, and compare purchase rates across the two groups using order records.
options.feedback: You remove returns, match both groups' assignment codes to the receipts, and ask the manager to run the numbers with you. The coupon group buys at a slightly higher rate, but Mei has to wait until closing for the report.
options.insight: The 2024 report puts first-party and member data at the center of the low-cookie era. Fragmented data and organizational silos remain barriers for retail media.

data.title: Who Gets Credit for the Sale?
data.brief: The meeting upstairs at Big Dawn Dome Broadcast Center is about to start. Su wants you to check one column: if the last click was on a digital ad, does digital get all the credit for the soy sauce order?

lines.text: You're the data analyst, right? Take a look. The boss circled the column that says ‘Orders driven by ads.’
I pulled the raw orders. That column only tells us which ad got the last click before checkout.
Got timestamps? I want to line them up with the station's airing logs.
I do. That breakfast shop on Wuxing Street ordered this very soy sauce. The owner said her grandson placed the order on his phone.
I'll ask her when she picked the brand. Kai, leave that order out of the rollup for now.

steps.hint: Wuxing St. Corner Breakfast Shop: what's everyone watching on TV?

lines.text: Hang on, the invoice is under the soy sauce bottle. I saw the ad during the news last night and told my grandson to buy that brand.
Did he click an ad on his phone before he ordered?
Sure did. He said there was a coupon if he clicked through. He even showed me.
I checked the airing log. The spot ran the night she asked him to buy it. The order came in the next day.
I'll put this order in a footnote. To see how many extra orders TV brought in, we need somewhere the spot didn't run to compare against.
Go ahead and snap a photo of the invoice. Pass me the soy sauce, would you? That egg pancake's about to burn.

steps.prompt: You've got one slide in the meeting. What numbers do you bring to the budget discussion?

options.text: Match redemptions to orders and fund digital placements with high coupon redemption rates.
options.feedback: More coupons get redeemed this week, and the retailer orders more stock on the spot. Next month, the client asks how new customers heard of the brand, and all you have are the clicks before checkout.
options.insight: The yearbook notes that algorithms favor people who are easiest to convert. Digital ads aimed only at a target group can also miss older people who do the household shopping.

options.text: Recalculate CPM on a common age range and keep broad-reach TV for the brand.
options.feedback: The boss drops the narrow age filter from the original sheet and signs off on next quarter's TV schedule. By month-end, more people remember the ad, and the client is still waiting to find out how many orders each channel actually drove.
options.insight: Dentsu estimates TV CPM at about 48 for ages 30 and up, while YouTube ads typically run 80–250. Narrow the TV audience to ages 30–39 and its CPM is about 247.

options.text: Pair similar areas and randomly pick one in each pair to get extra TV spots. Check retail sales and survey brand awareness.
options.feedback: You get the retailer to run the same promo on both sides and collect baseline sales. The client drops the claim that digital drives every conversion, but skipping an extra promo leaves sales behind target at month-end.
options.insight: The yearbook warns that a strong Brand Lift figure may just reflect people who already supported the brand.

data.title: How Many Times Did This Ticket Close?
data.brief: Right before the pitch, Lin asks you to check the returns agent’s case counts. The client has already used the chart to request a wider rollout.

lines.text: You’re the data analyst. Take a look at this chart. Buy First Select says case closures shot up as soon as the agent went live.
Support just dropped a screenshot in LINE. The customer’s still asking how to return the item, and the dashboard says it’s resolved.
I pulled the event log. Look at that. Same case ID, three close events.
The event got sent again. I matched the IDs to the support tickets, and once I took out the duplicates, the jump disappeared.
The client is signing off on the budget tomorrow morning. They want to lead the anniversary sale with “No waiting on returns.” Do I have them pull the copy now?
The people we’re pitching to are already in the A25 conference room. Swap out slide nine. What numbers are you taking in there?

steps.prompt: The duplicate closures are gone. What goes on slide nine?

options.text: Fast-track low-risk returns and use payment records to track exchange top-ups and repeat purchases.
options.feedback: Routine exchanges go faster, and the client sees repeat sales come in. Finance spots that most of the shoppers are regulars and asks you to strike “Fast-track returns drove repeat sales” from the deck.
options.insight: The yearbook warns that focusing solely on conversion rates can shift costs to support and logistics.

options.text: Randomly split similar cases between the current process and the new handoff rule.
options.feedback: You and Ah-Kai stay at A25 past the last train, linking reopened tickets and refunds back to the original cases. Early results show a lower reopen rate under the new rule, and the client agrees to expand the rollout.
options.insight: The yearbook cites an analysis of 200 B2B AI projects. Projects with a human in the loop had 104% higher ROI than fully automated ones.

options.text: Pause the rollout, spot-check tickets, and publish a corrected count with a way for customers to check their status.
options.feedback: You and Mei go through the sampled tickets one by one, and the brand adds a correction and a support link under the original post. Customers share the status link with other shoppers, but the sale loses its fast-returns hook and repeat orders drop.
options.insight: The yearbook describes three ways to build trust in AI agents: preview what they plan to do, audit what they did, and define when to hand off to a person.

cx.title: Who Gets the Points for This Coffee?
cx.brief: The hot Americano launches next week. Commuters at City Hall Station have seen the preorder pilot, and some have bought a cup. Manager Wu holds out a coffee sleeve and asks why staff are still sending customers back into the line.

lines.text: You're the e-commerce and loyalty consultant, right? Here, this sleeve is from yesterday's trial run.
I scanned one just like it at City Hall Bus Terminal. My phone made me sign up first. I almost closed the page when it asked for a verification code.
One of our regulars got all the way through payment. The cashier told her online orders don't earn points, so she lined up again to ask how to get hers credited.
She was probably trying to catch a bus, right? The sleeve even says 'ready when you get here.' Did support ever get her those points?
She asked again in the afternoon. Support can see her payment, but they have to call the store to check its points records.
Mind if I borrow this sleeve, Manager Wu? I want the first slide tonight to show what she went through, from scanning it to having to chase support.

steps.prompt: The hot Americano goes on sale next week. Manager Wu can fund one change. Where do you start?

options.text: Run a tasting outside the station and put a link to a shareable product page on the sleeves so commuters can discover the new coffee.
options.feedback: Photos of the tasting sleeves make it into nearby office group chats, and a company calls Manager Wu the next day about a group order. You spend the morning restocking sleeves and running the tasting table, while mobile shoppers still get stuck at the verification code.
options.insight: Posterscope found that 83% of shoppers had seen an out-of-home ad within 30 minutes before making a purchase.

options.text: Turn on guest checkout, show the pickup store and total on the first screen, and offer a coupon for the first cup.
options.feedback: Before lunch, customers are already paying on their phones and grabbing their Americanos on the way out of the station. You track pickup orders and coupon redemptions until close, and support is still asking how to credit those orders to loyalty accounts.
options.insight: Think with Google found that 53% of users abandon a mobile page if it takes longer than three seconds to load.

options.text: Pilot at one store near City Hall Station. Award points when staff scan the preorder pickup code, and let support look up missing points on LINE.
options.feedback: One scan gets the customer their coffee and their points, and yesterday's customer gets her missing points through LINE and preorders again the following week. Manager Wu asks you to show the other store managers how the pilot works and keeps next week's discount at the planned level.
options.insight: The yearbook cites an IDC retail report: retailers that use cross-channel strategies effectively can see profit growth of up to 35% and a 10% increase in customer loyalty.

cx.title: Stuck at Checkout
cx.brief: Searches for Itch Be Gone are down, and HQ wants to send members a coupon. Lin asks you to find out where shoppers drop off and why they go back to the convenience store.

lines.text: Seen the Itch Be Gone report? Searches are down, so HQ wants to send members a coupon at noon to lift sales.
A customer called yesterday. She tapped through from a Story, but at checkout the login code never came through.
I tried it on my phone. Checkout kicks me back to the login screen before the cart even shows shipping.
Her support ticket says she bought it last time at the convenience store on Songshou Road. I’ll ask the clerk how regulars restock.
Okay. By noon, I need one thing we can do. I’ll take it to HQ.

steps.hint: Songshou Rd. Corner Convenience Store: who's buying Itch Be Gone?

lines.text: A lady came in with an empty box this morning. She said the website kept asking her to log in, so she just came downstairs to buy it.
Is this where she bought it the first time, too?
Yep. Her shoes got soaked in the rain and she needed it right away. Now she comes straight in and asks if we have any.
If she comes all this way for nothing, she still has to dig out her password when she gets home. No wonder that ticket’s still open.
When we’re out, all I can do is send her to another store and hope for the best. Could your site help her ask who has it in stock first?

steps.prompt: Before heading back to A25, what do you ask HQ to tackle first?

options.text: Turn on guest checkout and apply the first-order discount right in the cart.
options.feedback: More orders come in that week, and support gets fewer calls about missing login codes. Returning members check out and then realize they didn’t get their points, so HQ has support credit each order by hand.
options.insight: The yearbook points out that when online stores optimize ads and neglect the shopping experience, shoppers tend to browse without buying or visit once and never return.

options.text: Fix member verification first and let support pull up the member’s cart when they take over.
options.feedback: Engineering spends three days fixing the text messages, and the promotion goes on hold. Support can now pick up where a shopper left off, and once HQ sees the callback logs, it puts you in charge of fixing the repeat-purchase experience.
options.insight: A survey found that 63% of consumers expect brands to use purchase history to personalize their experience. Only four in ten think brands deliver a consistent experience every time.

options.text: Pilot shelf cards in three convenience stores. Shoppers can scan to find a store and ask support to check stock.
options.feedback: Neighbors share the store finder in their local group chat, and some check stock before going out. In the first week, you have to go over the out-of-stock list with the stores every day, and online orders go up by just a few.
options.insight: The yearbook warns that relying only on the data that gets recorded can lead to bad calls. Sample surveys, retail interviews, and small data can show more of what customers actually do.

cx.title: The Refill Left in the Cart
cx.brief: Foot traffic is down at Manager Chen's stores. Regulars find their refills through LINE, then disappear before paying on the website. Before noon, the client can spare staff for one fix.

lines.text: Look at this screenshot. A customer followed the store's LINE link, picked a refill online, then went back to the clerk to ask how to buy it.
The clerk could see which one she'd bought in store. Support couldn't look it up by phone number, so they asked her for another photo of the bottom of the bottle.
Let me try it on my phone. I can see the shipping fee, but the second I hit checkout, it makes me sign up.
My boss just wants to know how many orders we lost this week. The order files are at Lanshan Plaza Data Lab. Can you take a look?
I'll go through them with Ah-Kai. Send me the time on that screenshot too. I want to see if she ever got her refill.

steps.hint: Go to Lanshan Plaza Data Lab and see if the client's data is usable

lines.text: Found it. She hit checkout twice that afternoon, then came back through the product page the next day. The refill was still in her cart. No order.
She actually came back for it. Can we pull what she bought in store into her online account?
We can start by verifying the phone number on her membership. The stores have to change their process too, or support will still be asking for bottle photos next week.
I'll put her shopping trip on the journey map. Manager Chen can see every step, from finding the refill on LINE to coming back for another one.

steps.prompt: The noon meeting will give one fix the go-ahead. What do you ask Manager Chen to do first?

options.text: Turn on guest checkout and run weekend ads offering free shipping on refills.
options.feedback: More carts make it through payment over the weekend. As soon as free shipping ends, people ask on the brand's page when the next deal is. Guest orders aren't linked to memberships, so support still has to dig up past orders to identify the right refill.
options.insight: The yearbook cites the Adidas case. Third-party research found that 65% of sales came from brand campaigns.

options.text: Let regulars link their store membership by verifying their phone number, so support can send them the name of their last refill and a reorder link.
options.feedback: On day one of the pilot, some texts don't come through, so you test with the store staff until closing. The following week, Manager Chen sees a support ticket where a regular used the reorder link to buy the same refill. Other stores have to wait until next month.
options.insight: The yearbook describes how Isobar introduced Salesforce and a new membership program for 10/10. In the first week, the program reached 8,880 LINE friends and a 74.61% member linking rate.

options.text: Have store staff show how to match old bottles to refills on a livestream, then turn it into a buying guide on the brand's site.
options.feedback: A few groups share the part about matching bottle openings, and the clerks start using the guide to answer questions. The free-shipping promo moves to next month and sales take a hit this week. You spend several evenings checking older bottles and stock with the store staff.
options.insight: The yearbook cites a Salesforce survey in which 84% of customers said the brand's content, interactions, and service at each touchpoint mattered as much as the product itself.

cx.title: Soup Left in the Cart
cx.brief: During Taiwan's Level 3 COVID alert, a trial livestream for frozen meal kits fills plenty of carts. Wei is at the Chillshan Creative Park studio, waiting for you to figure out where shoppers got stuck before you have to clear out at four.

lines.text: Everyone in the test stream was asking about the clam soup. The client says the carts just sat there once we went off air last night.
Wei, I tried it on my phone. You have to sign up before you can see shipping, and if you forget your password, you have to leave to check your email.
The member login is where we lost the most people last night. The logs can't tell me if it was the hassle or the cost of frozen shipping.
Support printed out last night's chats for me. One regular asked three times if they could change the delivery date, then said they'd order some other time.
I've put the stream link, the checkout screens, and the support tickets side by side. The launch is tonight, and the people who buy might come back for more next week.
We have to hand the studio back at four. The client will only pay for one plan today. Where do you want to start?

steps.prompt: Where in the customer journey should we spend the budget before the launch stream?

options.text: Keep the stream as planned. Add guest checkout, show the frozen shipping fee and delivery date up front, and give shoppers a way to reach a real person.
options.feedback: On launch night, some shoppers saw the shipping fee and went straight to payment. Support could focus on rescheduling deliveries, but the stream reused the product footage from the test and the buzz died down fast.
options.insight: The yearbook says the entire home commerce journey can happen from home. Brands need to get the details right, from running the shop online to delivering to the doorstep.

options.text: Turn the stream into a frozen parcel unboxing and show what to do if an order arrives thawed. Take down the buy link for now so support can focus on answering questions in the chat.
options.feedback: A support rep opened a box on camera and used a thermometer to show how to check an order on arrival. The clip made it into several neighborhood group chats, but orders that night fell short of the client's expectations.
options.insight: The yearbook features Sinyi Realty's “Trust and Happiness,” a campaign that deliberately sold no product. In post-testing, 70% of viewers showed a positive shift, compared with previous targets of 20 to 30%.

options.text: Shoot short clips on delivery and reheating. Show the shipping fee on the first-order page, then invite shoppers to join after paying and choose whether to get restock reminders.
options.feedback: Some viewers placed their first order after watching the reheating clip, while some members came back to restock after a reminder. You and Kai stayed up past midnight matching test orders to membership and support records one by one.
options.insight: In the 2020 CCS survey, 72.9% said they like brands that reward loyal customers, and 36.8% stick with a brand once they've settled on it.

cx.title: The Refill Stuck in the Cart
cx.brief: With the anniversary sale coming up, Manager Hsu lays out the support logs at the Shin Kong Mitsukoshi counter. Shoppers add the refill to their carts after watching a clip, then leave without paying. Few of the people who bought one come back for more.

lines.text: Look at this screenshot. A shopper tapped through from the unboxing clip, added a refill, and still had to ask support.
Let me try it on my phone. Shipping only shows up after I enter my address, and I have to go back to the product page to check whether my old bottle fits.
Plenty of people add it to their cart. We lose the most at the address page. As for why buyers never come back, the report can’t tell us that.
A customer brought her old bottle in yesterday. She’d bought a refill online, spilled it all over the table, and figured she’d just buy a new bottle this time.
Manager Hsu, let me match that receipt to the support log. Getting her through checkout and getting her to buy again are two different problems.
The anniversary sale starts next week. Manager Hsu has room in the budget for one change this week. Which part do you tackle first?

steps.prompt: Where do you spend the money first?

options.text: Apply a free-shipping voucher to refill carts automatically so shoppers see the reduced total before entering their address.
options.feedback: Over the weekend, some of the carts stalled at the address page turn into orders, and Manager Hsu posts them in the group chat. As soon as free shipping ends, someone comments on the product page that they’ll wait for the next voucher.
options.insight: The yearbook cites a Kantar LifePoints survey in which 85% of respondents thought eco-friendly products cost more. Convenience and cost kept 76% from taking action.

options.text: Show shipping costs and a bottle compatibility chart at checkout. Let support use the order to look up the bottle model and send a pouring guide.
options.feedback: On the first call after the pilot starts, support sends the right guide as soon as the customer gives their order number. Manager Hsu checks two older bottles against the page and signs off. Checking the bottle models takes three extra days, so the first anniversary-sale push notification still links to the old page.
options.insight: In the Kantar LifePoints survey, 71% of respondents said they had too little information. The yearbook also proposes using conversion rate optimization (CRO) to improve brand websites.

options.text: Ask repeat buyers to film how they pour refills at home. Let new shoppers book a pouring demo at the counter from the clip and pick when they want a restock reminder.
options.feedback: A member films herself pouring a refill through a silicone funnel, and a housekeeping group shares the clip. The comments fill up with people asking where to try it, and bookings outnumber orders at the counter that day. You spend the weekend matching names to bookings and answering DMs after closing.
options.insight: The yearbook names fragmented customer journeys as one of three types of fragmentation and calls for a shift from acquisition to retention. It also presents member segmentation and reactivating dormant customers as CRM applications.

cx.title: Chat Said Shipping Was Free
cx.brief: A frozen dumpling promo for members starts tomorrow morning. Ah-Kai is waiting at Lanshan Plaza. He wants you to run through the checkout on your phone.

lines.text: Can you try this? Tap the dumpling promo in LINE and ask support what shipping costs for two bags.
It says shipping's free. So why did a frozen shipping fee pop up right before payment?
Found it. The bot pulled last year's promo page. Two bags got you free shipping back then.
Look at this ticket. A regular thought the fee would come off when she signed in. She tried checking out three times, then asked if we'd changed her member perks.
The client wants the LINE message out at eight tomorrow. Their boss wants orders by the afternoon. If you're scaling it back, I need to call him now.
We've only got one engineer who can make changes tonight. Which part do you want to tackle first?

steps.prompt: Where do you send members when tomorrow's promo goes live?

options.text: Pause the push to checkout and go live with a cooking demo. Show people on your phone how the frozen shipping fee works.
options.feedback: You and the store manager stay up reshooting the cooking clip. The next day, people share the shipping demo in group-buy chats. The checkout link goes out a day late, and first-day orders take a hit.
options.insight: The yearbook warns that false content can do serious damage to a brand and calls for closer social listening.

options.text: Invite past buyers to try ordering first. Give the bot the current shipping table and hand off questions about combining coupons to a person.
options.feedback: Support can see the chat when they take over, so members don't have to resend their cart screenshots. One regular works out the shipping and adds two bags. For now, the offer stays with that first batch.
options.insight: The yearbook calls first-party data the foundation for making money with AI. Bad data in, bad results out.

options.text: Send a limited-time coupon for repeat buyers that takes them straight back to their carts. Clean up the old support answers after the promo.
options.feedback: The coupon brings in a rush of orders before dinner. Someone posts a screenshot of the bot promising free shipping, and the replies fill up with people asking whether the deal is real. You and support are still refunding shipping one order at a time after hours.
options.insight: The yearbook says generative AI is good at saving shoppers mental effort. Money, time, physical effort, and mental effort can all add friction to a purchase.

cx.title: The Jacket Still in the Cart
cx.brief: Shoppers at the new Linginger Street store scan the tags and leave without buying. Mei-ling asks you to try the whole journey before deciding where to spend the launch budget.

lines.text: One Less Piece opens next week. The client saw the soft-launch report and thinks one more coupon will get those jackets out of people's carts.
I pulled last night's logs. Several shoppers bailed at phone verification. They never even saw the payment page.
This is the kind of report I dread in e-commerce. They've picked a size. Why are we still making them sign up?
Follow the old shops to the shrine on Fude Street. The caretaker tried it on last night. Take this tag and ask him what happened.
Okay, I'll bring a test phone. I'll go through the exchange process too, as if the jacket had already arrived.

steps.hint: Walk the alleys to Fude St. Earth God Shrine. Note the old shops

lines.text: That's the one! My wife liked it on me. I scanned the tag, then it wanted me to check a text, so I just went home.
Look, I went all the way to the payment screen. I still can't find a number to call if the size is wrong.
Say I want to buy my brother the same jacket later. If I bring in the tag, will the staff know which one it is?
I'll write down the item number. Tonight's pitch needs to show how people can find the same jacket again after they buy it.

steps.prompt: Back at the flagship, there's room in the launch budget for one fix. Where do you spend it?

options.text: Run a two-night opening deal. Scan the tag to pay straight away. Discounted orders can be returned for a refund only.
options.feedback: Shoppers who'd dropped off at verification paid, and first-week orders beat the soft launch. One customer asked for the next size up, but support told her to return it and place a new order, so she turned off restock alerts too.
options.insight: The yearbook warns against chasing immediate traffic and sales. Building a brand over time helps sustain short-term results.

options.text: Borrow a mirror from the fabric shop for a neighborhood try-on. Make shareable fit cards with sizes and product links.
options.feedback: The fit cards made it into the neighborhood chat, and people came in with screenshots to ask about the jacket the next day. You and the staff checked sizes on every card until closing, and only a few orders came in that week.
options.insight: The yearbook reports that UNIQLO's East District partnership drew 2.2 times the previous year's visitors. 91% said the store would bring them to the district more often.

options.text: Offer guest checkout and print the exchange number on receipts. After purchase, let shoppers opt in to save their size in a member account.
options.feedback: The shrine caretaker called the number on his receipt. The clerk used the item number to set one aside for his brother. Repeat orders came in, but sign-ups grew slowly, and store staff and support had to take turns answering calls.
options.insight: The yearbook calls first-party and member data central to a world with fewer cookies. It also says customer experience needs to account for privacy and inclusion.

cx.title: I Scanned. Where’s the Soy Sauce?
cx.brief: The Big Dawn Dome Broadcast Center is launching a soy sauce sampler for its cooking show. Su asks you to find out where viewers get stuck after scanning the code, before the meeting upstairs.

lines.text: The soy sauce sampler goes live right after tonight’s cooking show. Could you take a look at these comments?
Scanning the code in rehearsal took people straight to sign-up. Someone’s already asked support, “Do I need an account just to buy one bottle?”
Let me scan it. The page doesn’t even show shipping yet. No wonder people are closing it.
The boss wants to see how many sets we sell tonight. You’ve got twenty minutes before the meeting upstairs. Ask the auntie at the corner shop. She scanned it too.

steps.hint: Wuxing St. Corner Breakfast Shop: what's everyone watching on TV?

lines.text: Those braised tofu bites looked good on TV, so I scanned it. My egg was burning on the griddle by the time the code came.
If you could check out first, how would you order another bottle when this one runs out?
I’d pull up the order and look for the same bottle. Last time support asked for a product number. How was I supposed to know where to find that?
I’ll sketch out what you just went through on the back of this order slip. I’m taking it upstairs.

steps.prompt: Before you head upstairs, Su asks what you’d change first tonight. What will you do for viewers who scan?

options.text: Open guest checkout tonight, apply the first-order discount automatically, and invite shoppers to join later.
options.feedback: First orders jump that night, and the boss takes the shipping slips over to sales. The following week, shoppers come back looking for the deal and can’t even remember the soy sauce brand.
options.insight: The yearbook says too many offers and loyalty programs can make decisions harder, prompting shoppers to turn to agents for help choosing.

options.text: Send viewers who scan to the show’s braised tofu recipe, let them add the soy sauce to their cart there, and cut a short clip to bring people back.
options.feedback: The next day someone shares the recipe in a LINE group and asks where to buy that soy sauce. The editor stays after the show to finish the clip, and orders come in more slowly on opening night than with an immediate discount.
options.insight: The yearbook says brands should make content that fits each platform and stay recognizable as audiences move across screens.

options.text: Start with a small run, show shipping up front, let support reorder from the original order, and give members the option to get reminders.
options.feedback: The boss agrees to a trial, but cutting the first night’s stock leaves sales short of target. You work the late shift with support to practice repeat orders. The next week, a shopper gives the last four digits of her order number and support finds her original bottle.
options.insight: The yearbook lists check-ins, journey maps that flag drop-off points, and playbooks for returning customers as ways to see where customers get stuck.

cx.title: How Do I Buy the Next Box?
cx.brief: Buy First Select uses AI to help customers restock. Some get stuck at member sign-in, while others place an order and only then realize their points weren't applied. Lin wants your call on the weekend rollout before the pitch.

lines.text: It's nine. Keep your laptop open. Buy First Select is pushing skincare reorders this weekend, and their e-commerce lead is waiting for our go-ahead.
I followed the unboxing clip all the way to checkout. Look, she tries to use her points and gets kicked back to the sign-in screen.
I told the AI to repeat my last order on a test account. It used the free shipping coupon. I only saw that it hadn't applied my points after the order went through.
Support has a ticket about that exact thing. Pickup at the convenience store went fine last time. Now she says she'll just buy it in person next time.
I'll put that ticket on slide nine. She already knew which box she wanted. She just needed to see what she was getting before the order went through.
They're calling us into the meeting room. We've got one version for the weekend. How far do you let the shopping assistant go?

steps.prompt: Get back to the e-commerce lead before the pitch. How should members check out when they buy their next box this weekend?

options.text: Repeat the last order, with the shopping assistant applying the free shipping coupon and placing the order.
options.feedback: Reorders start stacking up in the convenience-store pickup queue first thing Saturday. By afternoon, support is taking cancellations from members who got free shipping and realized they hadn't used the points they meant to spend.
options.insight: The 2026 report cites Baymard Institute data putting the global average cart abandonment rate at about 70.2%.

options.text: Preview the discount and pickup details first. If points and the coupon can't be used together, pass the cart to a support rep.
options.feedback: You and Ah-Kai run a test account all the way to payment and only remember your dinner when you leave the meeting room. Over the weekend, the rep can see the cart as soon as they take over, and the customer uses her points to buy her second box on the spot.
options.insight: The report's section on agent experience (AX) describes three parts of designing for trust: previewing intent, auditing actions, and giving users a way to escalate.

options.text: Pause automated orders and have support demo member discounts and convenience-store pickup on the unboxing livestream.
options.feedback: Support uses a receipt on the livestream to show how to choose a discount, and viewers clip and share that bit. You're still staring at the weekly report at midnight: more chatter, a lot fewer reorders.
options.insight: The report cites DHL's social commerce research, which found that 70% of consumers have bought directly on social media.
